Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of valorization pathways for drill cuttings and rock fragments, spanning oil and gas, core/ROV, and mining contexts, along with environmental, technical, and regulatory considerations.

# What are drill cuttings and rock fragments, and why valorize them?

Drill cuttings are the rock and mineral fragments removed from a borehole and returned to the surface during drilling, typically mixed with drilling fluid (mud) and subsequently managed as waste unless reused or treated. <cite id="7750b458-1">Construction of offshore oil and gas wells generates large volumes of waste, particularly drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids, posing risks of marine environmental contamination; oilfield drilling fluids and cuttings can carry hydrocarbons and heavy metals</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-4">Traditionally, non-biological disposal routes included burial pits, landfills, reinjection, chemical stabilization/solidification, and thermal treatments (incineration, thermal desorption), with more recent additions of bioremediation</cite>. <cite id="7750b447-0">Contaminated cuttings can be decontaminated and valorized for reuse in civil construction or repurposed as adsorbents/catalysts for pollutant removal in environmental applications</cite>.

Rock fragments arise not only in oil and gas drilling but also in scientific core drilling (ROV/vibrocoring), mining, and polar geology. <cite id="c56cbe8d-1">ROV-based rock drills and vibrocorers retrieve cores up to 5–6 m in hard rock or soft sediments with water depths up to 2000–6000 m, emphasizing orientation and high-quality sample recovery</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">In ICDP coring operations, a solids-removal/recycling unit recycles drilling fluid and returns cuttings and fluid to the hole, reducing environmental impact and improving cost efficiency</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-4">Wireline coring tools latch and unlatch core barrels to recover ice and rock cores without pulling the entire string, illustrating engineered workflows for rock fragment retrieval and solids handling</cite>.

Valorization addresses material scarcity of high-quality aggregates and binder modifiers, waste-disposal constraints, and environmental risk from hydrocarbons and metals. <cite id="7750b458-1">A holistic review highlights that valorization in civil construction is prominent, with growing use of thermal/chemical pretreatments and a lack of standardized regulation across jurisdictions</cite>.

# Environmental and operational drivers for valorization

Oilfield drill cuttings can leach hydrocarbons and heavy metals, prompting ecological risk and cleanup burdens. <cite id="7750b458-1">Environmental risks include toxicity, bioaccumulation, and contamination by hydrocarbons and heavy metals; characterization and risk assessment are needed to guide reuse</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-4">Bioremediation and other treatments are being applied to reduce contamination before reuse or disposal</cite>. In scientific and mining drilling, solids-control systems recycle cuttings and mud to protect water columns and reduce waste. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">A Heli-Portable Solids Removal Unit recycles drilling fluid and reintroduces cleaned fluid to the borehole, and variable drilling-fluid programs with LCM manage losses while returning cuttings to the drill floor for reuse</cite>.

Marine operations also consider dispersants and site-specific risk. <cite id="7750b458-1">Contaminated cuttings pose marine contamination risks; integrated strategies combining treatment, reuse, and risk assessment are urged to mitigate offshore pollution</cite>.

# Construction and civil-engineering valorization

Concrete and cement-based products offer scalable reuse, with performance that improves with appropriate treatment and blending.

- As cement replacement or mineral additive:
  <cite id="68b61b20-0">Replacing 5–35% cement with drill cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, 22%, and 63% in tests directly comparing specimens; however, replacing 10–20% cement with drill cuttings showed no significant effect on compressive strength, suggesting 20% cement replacement as an optimum in that study</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-3">Replacing 5% cement with dried cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, while 10–20% replacements reduced strength by 20%, with significant improvements when additives like fly ash and silica fume were included</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-4">These additives significantly influenced the compressive strength of mixes with 20% drill cuttings</cite>.

- As treated aggregates or fillers:
  <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings at 5–20% replacement (w/b = 0.5; mix 1:1.5:3) achieved 26.2–22.5 N/mm² at 28 days, exceeding minimums for C/20–C/25; 28-day strength activity indices of 90.6–77.6% surpassed the 75% code minimum; wet/dry durability and leachability (chlorides and TPAHs) met reuse targets; pozzolanic activation at 500°C for 180 min improved performance</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Literature reports high compressive strength when drill cuttings form 50–80% of a base course aggregate, and mixes with 20% cement+80% cuttings show stable strength; partially substituting 10–20% sand with cuttings in bricks and concrete produced technically adequate building materials</cite>.

- Design guidance:
  <cite id="68b61b20-0">Incorporating drill cuttings as a partial cement replacement can lower costs, but strength loss grows sharply at higher substitution ratios; 20% cement replacement emerged as a practical upper bound without significant loss in that study</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Pozzolanic activation and optimized w/b (~0.5) mitigate strength reduction and improve durability and leachability compliance</cite>.

Beyond concrete, oilfield cuttings and rock fines can be used as aggregate or filler in bricks, pavers, and blocks, and as raw material for cinder blocks and paving slabs. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Drill cuttings have been used as filler or binder in bricks and concrete, and as aggregate for road bases, with stable strength properties at high inclusion levels</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Using drill cuttings as filler replacement yields lower-grade concrete suitable for foundation blinding, walling, and fill, while additives like fly ash/silica fume can upgrade properties</cite>.

Asphalt and bitumen-modified mixes offer another avenue, leveraging hydrocarbons and filler characteristics.

- Bitumen modification and aggregate replacement:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-2">Asphalt (bitumen) binder protects and binds aggregates; additives/modifiers are used to improve adhesion, reduce mixing/compaction temperatures, and increase resistance to cracking and rutting</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-3">Adding 15% granulated rubber stiffens the binder (penetration shifts from 50/70 to 35/50) and improves temperature susceptibility; rubber addition increases the penetration index, lowers phase angle, and improves elastic properties, confirming better resistance to temperature susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Two large-tonnage wastes suitable for asphalt concrete are drill cuttings (containing rock plus up to ~5% oil) and plastics; the oil provides light hydrocarbons that increase bitumen adhesion and reduce aging rate, and cuttings can be used as mineral powder or for paving slabs, curbs, cinder blocks, road components, and organo-mineral mixtures</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-1">Crumb rubber is commonly incorporated by dry-mixing with aggregates for 2-minute blending followed by Marshall compaction, illustrating practical integration of hydrocarbon-rich fillers into binders and mixes</cite>.

- Practical implications:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Because drill cuttings contain oil and angular rock particles, they can act both as a mineral powder and as a source of hydrocarbons that enhance adhesion and slow aging in bitumen; preliminary assessments suggest feasibility as an aggregate or filler with cost reductions and reduced accumulation</cite>.

# Environmental applications: adsorbents, soil conditioners, and catalysts

Contaminated drill cuttings can be decontaminated and repurposed for environmental remediation.

- Adsorbents and catalyst supports:
  <cite id="7750b458-0">Decontaminated drill cuttings have been used as adsorbents and catalysts for pollutant removal from wastewater, and global-scale treatment/valorization solutions have been proposed</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Valorization routes in civil construction and environmental applications are explored in recent reviews, with patent analyses showing growth in thermal/chemical pretreatments that enable reuse</cite>.

- Soil and land uses:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Drill cuttings can be formed into soil-agrarian mixtures and used as components in organo-mineral mixtures for construction and agriculture, leveraging oil content to improve adhesion and reduce aging</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Bricks and permeable bricks with 10–20% cuttings substitution are technically adequate for building construction, indicating potential for landscaping and non-load-bearing applications</cite>.

These applications benefit from pre-treatment (e.g., thermal activation) to enhance pozzolanicity or surface area and to reduce leachability of contaminants. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Activation at 500°C for 180 minutes improved pozzolanic activity and enabled up to 20% cement replacement without significant strength loss while meeting leachability targets</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Risk assessments and treatment technologies are emphasized to ensure environmental acceptability</cite>.

# Industrial and energy-sector valorization

- Oil/bitumen binder recovery and modification:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Drill cuttings contain up to ~5% oil, which can serve as light hydrocarbon adhesion promoters in bitumen, reducing aging and improving performance in asphalt concrete and related products</cite>.

- Drilling fluid solids control and reintegration:
  <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Mining and scientific coring use solids removal units to return cleaned drilling fluid to the hole and recycle cuttings, reducing environmental footprint and material waste</cite>. In oil and gas, hydrocyclones, centrifuges, and desanders separate reusable solids from mud, enabling re-use of filtrate and return of clean cuttings to the hole or to aggregates processing lines, depending on specifications. <cite id="7750b458-4">Solidification/stabilization and thermal desorption are used to condition cuttings for safe reuse or disposal, and bioremediation has been successfully applied</cite>.

- Backfill and structural fill:
  <cite id="68b61b20-2">Mixtures with 20% cement and 80% drill cuttings demonstrated stable strength properties suitable for road construction, indicating applicability to base/stabilized fills and low-to-medium load bases</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">Filler-grade applications can be supported by additives like fly ash to offset strength loss at higher cuttings fractions</cite>.

# Scientific and geotechnical rock fragment valorization

Scientific coring produces oriented rock cores that can be used for structural, geochemical, and material studies, and the cuttings can be returned to the environment or processed for specific uses. <cite id="c56cbe8d-0">An ROV-based coring tool with an inner non-rotating pipe and chip marks produces oriented cores in soft rocks like limestone, enabling detailed structural analysis</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-2">TV-guided vibrocoring with multiple core barrels (e.g., 10 cm diameter, 50 cm depth) yields high-quality crustal rock samples used for geological and physical property characterization</cite>.

These systems emphasize low-impact operations and solids handling that support reuse. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Recycling units and LCM programs return cuttings and fluid to the hole, reducing environmental impact; solids-control strategies are tailored to borehole conditions</cite>. In permafrost and polar drilling, specialized coring tools and fluid management prevent thermal instability and enable material recovery for construction or environmental management. <cite id="c56cbe8d-4">Ice/rock core recovery tools latch core barrels and circulate drilling fluid, facilitating retrieval without pulling the entire string; this workflow yields intact rock fragments for subsequent reuse</cite>.

# Circular-economy strategies, barriers, and regulatory context

Integrated management is key. <cite id="7750b458-1">A holistic strategy combining characterization, risk assessment, treatment, and legal alignment is needed; reviews emphasize the scarcity of integrated approaches and growing use of thermal/chemical processes, alongside heterogeneous national regulations</cite>.

Technical barriers include variability in composition, contamination, and durability concerns. <cite id="7750b458-1">Drill cuttings vary by formation and fluid chemistry, carrying hydrocarbons and metals that require risk-based management to protect ecosystems and human health</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Strength retention and leachability constraints typically allow up to 20% cement replacement with treated cuttings for structural concrete; beyond this, additives or treatment are required</cite>.

Process and quality control are critical. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Using drill cuttings in asphalt concrete as mineral powder or reinforcing/bitumen modifier requires preliminary assessment of particle size and properties to ensure compatibility and performance</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Operational strategies (HP-SRU, LCM, variable fluid programs) control loss circulation and solids handling, enabling reuse of cuttings and fluid</cite>.

Economic and market barriers include certification, standards, and supply chain integration. <cite id="7750b458-1">Legal/regulatory comparisons reveal a lack of standardized norms for reuse across jurisdictions, which complicates large-scale valorization</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-0">Despite innovation, integrated reviews note the need to link drilling technical complexity with quantitative characterization and reuse pathways</cite>.

# Practical roadmap and examples

- Pre-treatment and qualification:
  <cite id="68b61b20-1">Screening for hydrocarbon and metal leachates; thermal/chemical activation (e.g., 500°C/180 min) to enhance pozzolanicity and durability; target 28-day strength activity indices ≥75–90% for structural uses</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Risk assessment and environmental characterization should precede reuse, with compliance to disposal and reuse regulations</cite>.

- Construction reuse targets:
  - Concrete: <cite id="68b61b20-1">Use treated drill cuttings at 5–20% as cement replacement with w/b ~0.5; 20% is often an upper bound without significant strength loss when additives like fly ash are used</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">At 20% cement replacement, strength may decrease by ~20%, but cost and embodied carbon can be reduced</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">For base course and non-structural uses, 50–80% cuttings in aggregate mixes can yield adequate compressive strength</cite>.
  - Asphalt: <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Use cuttings as mineral powder or integrate oil-rich fines to improve bitumen adhesion and resistance to aging; preliminary tests suggest feasibility with performance comparable to conventional mixes when particle size is controlled</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-3">Rubber-modified binders demonstrate improved temperature susceptibility and elastic properties, illustrating the broader class of hydrocarbon-modified fillers</cite>.

- Environmental reuse:
  <cite id="7750b458-0">After decontamination, drill cuttings can serve as adsorbents/catalysts for wastewater treatment; pilot and case-study programs have demonstrated scalability</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">For bricks and permeable pavers, 10–20% cuttings substitution is technically adequate for building applications, expanding market reach</cite>.

- Scientific/industrial integration:
  <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Adopt solids-removal/recycling systems to return clean cuttings and mud to operations, reducing environmental impact and enabling reuse as aggregates or fillers on site</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-1">For ROV/coring programs, co-produce oriented cores for research and manage cuttings with vibrocorers to enable reuse in construction or environmental applications</cite>.

# Key takeaways and remaining gaps

Valorization pathways exist across construction, environmental remediation, and industrial recovery, with demonstrated performance in concrete and asphalt when materials are characterized and treated appropriately. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings can replace up to 20% of cement in structural concrete while meeting strength and durability criteria, provided w/b and activation are optimized</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Oil-bearing drill cuttings can improve bitumen adhesion and reduce aging when used as modifiers or mineral powder in asphalt concrete</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-0">Decontaminated cuttings can be deployed as adsorbents and catalysts for pollution control</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Solids-control integration in mining and marine drilling enables closed-loop reuse of cuttings and mud</cite>.

Critical gaps to resolve at scale include standardized pre-treatment protocols, durable long-term performance data for structural uses, and harmonized regulatory frameworks. <cite id="7750b458-1">Reviews emphasize the scarcity of integrated strategies and regulatory standardization, calling for combined treatment–reuse approaches and risk assessments</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Field-scale durability and environmental leachability monitoring are needed beyond lab curing to validate lifetimes</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">Economic valuation studies that compare lifecycle costs of disposal versus valorized products (including carbon and energy footprints) would strengthen adoption</cite>.

In practice, a site-specific valorization plan should combine solids control, decontamination/activation, product design (e.g., 5–20% cement or binder replacement), and compliance with environmental and civil-engineering standards, while leveraging the inherent properties of drill cuttings/rock fragments (angular interlock, mineralogy, and hydrocarbon content) to create circular value. <cite id="7750b458-1">Integrated strategies that align treatment, reuse, and regulation are central to sustainable management</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings have shown adequate structural performance and leachability compliance at 5–20% replacement, with activation improving activity indices</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Oil content in cuttings can be harnessed to improve bitumen performance in asphalt mixes, expanding reuse horizons</cite>.

Snippet: Abstract Increasing the need of energy and its high price tempts companies to drill more oil wells every day and create more drilling waste. Most of these drilling wastes are managed to be disposed but they will always have many environmental impacts. Therefore, this study investigates the potential of using drill cuttings in concrete as a partial replacement of cement. The innovation of this study is not only to produce a new and cost-effective material from drill cuttings, but also to mitigate its negative environmental impacts. To achieve this objective, laboratory studies carried out to quantify the compressive strength of concrete samples and to determine the chemical composition of drill cuttings. Results showed that replacing 5% of cement with dried drill cuttings reduces the compressive strength of concrete by 10%. However, comprehensive strength of concrete samples decreases by 20% when replacing 10, 15, and 20% of cement with drill cuttings. Furthermore, the effect of some additives such as fly ash and silica fume on the compressive strength of the concrete samples containing drill cuttings was studied. Title: Rotation of the Philippine Sea plate inferred from paleomagnetism of oriented cores taken with an ROV-based coring apparatus
Snippet: An ROV-based coring apparatus recently developed by KOKEN BORING MACHINE CO. LED. was used for taking oriented cores from the seafloor (Fig. 2a). The maximum penetration length is 37 cm, which enables to drill target rocks covered with relatively thick manganese (Mn) crust. The core diameter is 3 cm. The drilling rod consists of an inner pipe and an outer pipe with a drill bit (Fig. 2b). The inner pipe does not rotate, which enables coring of soft rocks such as limestone. The inside of the inner pipe is not straight but slightly inclined at a certain point of the pipe to snap off a core from bedrock. The inner pipe has a hard chip at its entrance to mark an orientation line to a core (Fig. 2d). The direction and inclination of the orientation line are measured with a sensor unit (a magnetic compass and inclinometer) placed on the frame of the corer. Using this technique, we can obtain fully oriented cores such as those used for onshore paleomagnetic research. Refer Tajima et al. (2020) for more information of the coring apparatus.
</snippet>

Title: British geological survey remotely operated sea bed rockdrills and vibrocorers: new advances to meet the needs of the scientific community
Snippet: The British Geological Survey (BGS) built their first remotely operated rock drill in the late 1960s. CONSUB (Fig. 1) was a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) capable of retrieving short cores from the seabed. It was decommissioned in the early 1970s to be replaced by the midi-drill. The midi-drill (1975The midi-drill ( -1983 was capable of acquiring cores up to 1m long and was constrained to shallower water depths. As scientific exploration moved into deeper water a new version of the rock drill (RD1) was designed and built in-house (Fig. 2). RD1 is a combined rockdrill and vibrocoring system offering the flexibility of two sampling systems in one rig to the scientific and commercial communities. RD1 is capable of retrieving cores up to 5m long in "hard rock" via traditional rotary coring techniques and cores up to 6m long in "soft sediment" environments in vibrocorer mode. The maximum operational water depth for the RD1 system is 2000m. The RD1 system has been operational since 1982 and is still in use today. The Oriented Drill was specifically designed to recover samples for use in palaeomagnetic studies and was initially developed for use on the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) funded BRIDGE Programme (British Mid-Ocean Ridge Programme;1996-1998 on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The maximum core length is 0.8m and the maximum operational water depth of the drill is 5500m. Orientation is achieved by scribing the core along its length with a single reference line and then using the two drill-mounted compasses to assign a heading to this reference mark. This mark can then be related to a world reference thereby facilitating detailed palaeomagnetic analysis.

The BGS have designed, built and operated vibrocorers since the 1970s and are the BGS's oldest form of powered coring device with a long and successful track record of recovering high-quality samples worldwide from Greenland to the Scottish fjords. The system can be configured for 3m, 4m or 6m maximum core lengths and can operate in maximum water depths of 2000m via the BGS umbilical winch or 6000m water depth using the new battery-operated system (Fig. 3).

Title: Expedition 364 methods
Snippet: The coring rig utilized was the International Continental Scientific Drilling Project (ICDP) Atlas Copco T3WDH mining rig, utilizing flush-jointed mining drill strings and a modified top drive. The rig had a mast capable of handling 6 m string lengths, and coring was conducted using a specially built coring top drive system installed in the mast (Figure F6). Wireline operation of the core barrel was conducted through broken, locked drill string. The coring rig was cantilevered off the bow of the L/B Myrtle (Figure F4). The drilling and coring plan was carefully designed to allow the greatest number of options for casing, drill rod/barrel, and core diameters. 

An AMC Heli-Portable Solids Removal Unit (HP-SRU) was utilized to reduce the environmental impact and cost efficiency of the hole through a drilling fluid recycling system. Cuttings and drilling fluid were returned to the drill floor once open-hole drilling commenced. The drilling fluid was cleaned and filtered within the HP-SRU. The cleaned drilling fluid was added to a batch of newly mixed drilling fluid before being returned to the borehole. At 79 m DSF, drilling fluid did not return to the drill floor due to a loss of circulation. Below this depth, the remainder of the open-hole interval was drilled using seawater, with the occasional addition of drilling mud to reduce friction. 

The HP-SRU was also used in the cored interval. A variable drilling fluid program comprising combinations of seawater, mud products, and loss circulation material (LCM) was used, depending on borehole conditions. Several zones of lost circulation were encountered. Goff et al., (2016). Regional bathymetry from Amante et al., (2009).

Title: Agile Sub-Ice Geological (ASIG) Drill development and Pirrit Hills field project
Snippet: Tanner Kuhl and others surface of the reamers includes diamond-impregnated surfaces with zero borehole clearance separated by waterways for drilling fluid circulation. The TK56 wireline coring tools allow a core barrel assembly to be alternately latched and unlatched into the BHA to recover ice and rock core to the surface without having to pull the entire drill string every run (Fig. 7a). The core barrel assembly is pumped down with normal circulating drill fluid to the BHA, where it automatically latches into the outer core barrel (Fig. 7b). An optional dry-hole lowering device can be used to trip the inner core barrel assembly to the bottom using the wireline winch. The bottom of the inner core barrel, which sits directly behind  the coring bit face when latched into the outer core barrel, contains a split-ring tapered core lifter that grips the core (ice and rock) when the drill string is lifted slightly during core break and retains the core in the inner core barrel. The wireline winch is used in conjunction with an overshot to connect to the core barrel head assembly at the top of the inner core barrel, unlatch the head assembly from the outer core barrel and pull the core barrel assembly to the surface. Core barrels are available for 1.5 and 3 m core lengths. 

Several fishing tools are available to help retrieve broken tooling from the borehole. Tapered recovery taps with sharp, righthand threads are available for both drill pipe and casing. They are run downhole on drill pipe and rotated to thread into the top of broken or dropped pipe/casing for retrieval. An expanding recovery tap can also be used for recovering drill pipe without rotation. A casing cutter is included with ASIG for cutting off stuck casing that cannot be otherwise retrieved. It is run downhole on drill pipe and features a milling cutter that expands   Drilling fluid can be removed from a borehole with a swab assembly or with a bailer. Title: Review of Mixing Mechanism and Performance of Natural Rubber with Bituminous Materials
Snippet: One of the first known materials utilized in engineering is bitumen.Bitumen has been applied in several ways, such as an adhesive, waterproofing agent, pavement binder, and sealer.As time went on, bitumen's use spread quickly around the world, with pavement construction being its predominant use.Most roads with conventional asphalt function well, but when demands on them rise annually, and inadequate maintenance causes pavement degradation and a reduction in total life.Conventional asphalt may often lead to significant pavement failures, such as fatigue, ravelling, low temperature cracking, and strapping failures, when combined with extreme weather and high traffic.Asphalt binder becomes stiff at low temperatures and has a tendency to break under stress because of its temperature sensitivity.One strategy to improve the functionality of asphalt pavement is to modify the bitumen.In addition to polymer modified asphalt, or PMA, there are alternative methods that include modification using fillers such as fly ash, hydrated lime, carbon black and others.Nonetheless, PMA modification is one of the significant ways to improve road pavement.Prior research has yielded promising outcomes regarding bitumen modified with polymers, underscoring the use of polymers in bitumen, an area of considerable attention in recent times.The primary advantage of polymer technology is in its ability to enhance the bonding properties between bitumen and aggregate, resulting in a significant improvement in the efficiency of traditional bitumen [1].By creating an aggregate coating material, polymermodified bitumen enhanced the degree of cohesion, adhesion, and surface roughness of aggregates, leading to better bitumen mixes.

The objective of this review article is to thoroughly assess the process of adding epoxidized natural rubber, natural rubber latex and cup lump natural rubber to conventional bitumen in order to improve the result of rheological, chemical, and physical mixes qualities for improved road performance.As indicated in previous studies, the direct mixing approach and use of some chemical solvent and addition of additives are discussed.We highlight their application on bitumen modification and their noteworthy improvements to bitumen that has been changed.Furthermore, this research concentrates on the addition of xylene and toluene as a solvent for rubber treatment in order to guarantee the homogeneity of the rubber mixture.
</snippet>

Title: Life Cycle Assessment for the Production Phase of Nano-Silica-Modified Asphalt Mixtures
Snippet: Asphalt is the most widely used pavement layer in the world. It consists of a binding material called bitumen and crushed or natural aggregates. The mixture of these materials forms asphalt mixtures. Demand for paved roads exceeded the supply of lake asphalts in the late 1800s and led to the use of petroleum asphalts [1]. Asphalt is often used as a shortened form of asphalt concrete which is the material of choice in the pavement sector. In the United Kingdom and the rest of Europe, the term 'bitumen' is used as a synonym for the term 'asphalt binder' while 'asphalt cement' is often used in the United States [2]. Asphalt cement or bitumen is used to bind the aggregates together to provide the required strength and stiffness to transfer vehicular loads. In addition to its strength and stiffness, asphalt pavements offer a damping ability due to the viscous-elastic nature of the bitumen [3]. Consequently, asphalt mixtures are qualified to provide optimal driving comfort as well as flexible maintenance actions. Asphalt pavements are designed to provide maximum performance throughout the design life. Bitumen (asphalt binder) performs two functions: Binding aggregates together and protecting the aggregates from distortions. However, unlike concrete pavements, asphalt pavements experience deformations over short periods of time. This, coupled with increased traffic loads and extreme weather conditions have resulted in asphalt pavement authorities seeking alternative solutions to improve the resistance of the road pavements to the adverse effects of mechanical and environmental loading [4]. 

Currently, several additives and modifiers produced commercially are used to modify the properties of the asphalt binder. Ref. [3] stated that additives and other modifiers are added in asphalt mixtures to lower mixing and compaction temperatures. This was found to improve adhesion and increase resistance against cracking and rutting. Regarding the viscosity of bitumen, Ref. [5] studied the effects of asphaltene on rheological properties of diluted Athabasca bitumen. Nanotechnology and nanomaterials have recently attracted significant attention from the pavement industry. Nanomaterial application is considered to have the potential to improve asphalt binder properties.
</snippet>

Title: Assessment of temperature susceptibility for rubber granulate modified road asphalt binders considering impact of aging
Snippet: The following conclusions can be formulated on the basis of the results of tests performed for activated and inactivated rubber modified asphalt binders. a) Addition of granulated rubber (both activated and inactivated) has an influence on raising the softening point and reduction of 50/70 bitumen penetration, which causes a shift of the bitumen in classification concerning penetration determined at 25°C from type 50/70 to 35/50, which means that in result of rubber addition, bitumen has been stiffened. Similar changes in asphalt binder stiffness can be observed on the basis of analysis of the impact of short and long term aging, however, in this case the changes are smaller than for unaged bitumen. b) Addition of rubber to 50/70 penetration grade bitumen causes an increase in the value of the analyzed binder penetration index, both before and after short and long time aging, whereas the lowest values of penetration index was found for the reference bitumen, whereas the highest for inactivated rubber modified asphalt binder. This proves that addition of rubber has a positive impact on a decrease in temperature susceptibility of the analyzed binder which is a desirable effect. c) The process of aging improves temperature susceptibility of investigated asphalt binders through increasing penetration index PI (the highest values were obtained for asphalt binders after RTFOT and PAV aging) and shear modulus index SMI (the highest values were found for asphalt binders after RTFOT aging). d) Addition of 15% of rubber (activated and inactivated) leads to reduction of the dynamic shear modulus value at low temperatures and its increase at high road pavement operational temperatures which confirms a positive impact of the rubber addition on asphalt binders temperature susceptibility. e) Addition of activated and inactivated rubber contributes to a decrease in asphalt binder phase angle. This decrease is most visible for the high pavement operational temperatures (over 30°C). On this basis, it can be concluded that addition of rubber causes improvement of the binder elastic properties.
</snippet>

Title: The use of waste in the composition of organic-mineral mixtures used in road construction
Snippet: Another option for the successful use of waste in the composition of asphalt concrete is the use of specific properties of waste, which can increase the strength or other characteristics of asphalt concrete. [15][16][17][18] An example is the use of polymer waste as modifiers of bitumen (to improve the adhesion of bitumen to mineral components), waste cellulose, asbestos, plastic as a reinforcing additive (to increase strength, wear resistance, resistance to rutting). [19,20] These wastes have no chemical relationship with natural components used in asphalt concrete, but improve the characteristics of asphalt concrete due to the formation of new bonds in the structure of asphalt concrete. 

Using the above mentioned principles of waste selection for use in the composition of roadbuilding materials, two large-tonnage waste can be distinguished, which can be successfully used in the composition of asphalt concrete. These are drill cuttings (oil drilling waste) and plastic waste (low and high pressure polyethylene). Drilling cuttings contain rock and up to 5% oil. The oil content depends on the geological conditions, the technical condition of the drilling equipment, and the work culture. In this case, oil is considered as a source of light hydrocarbons capable of increasing the adhesion properties of bitumen and reducing the rate of aging of bitumen during the technological cycle of asphalt concrete production and operation. Using drill cuttings it is possible to obtain: paving slabs; curbs; concrete mixes; components for road surface; cinder blocks used in the construction of utility rooms; organo-mineral mixtures used in construction; soil-agrarian mixtures for agricultural use; ceramic brick. Based on a preliminary assessment of the physical and mechanical properties and particle size distribution, it was suggested that drill cuttings could be used as a mineral powder in asphalt concrete. At the same time, a reduction in the cost of asphalt concrete production will be achieved and the volume of accumulation of drill cuttings will decrease. 

Waste plastic, when used in asphalt concrete, can play the role of a reinforcing element and bitumen modifier, which will improve the performance of asphalt concrete. Plastics based on HDPE and LDPE have a melting point sufficient to create monolithic organo-mineral structures.

Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of valorization pathways for drill cuttings and rock fragments, spanning oil and gas, core/ROV, and mining contexts, along with environmental, technical, and regulatory considerations.

# What are drill cuttings and rock fragments, and why valorize them?

Drill cuttings are the rock and mineral fragments removed from a borehole and returned to the surface during drilling, typically mixed with drilling fluid (mud) and subsequently managed as waste unless reused or treated. <cite id="7750b458-1">Construction of offshore oil and gas wells generates large volumes of waste, particularly drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids, posing risks of marine environmental contamination; oilfield drilling fluids and cuttings can carry hydrocarbons and heavy metals</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-4">Traditionally, non-biological disposal routes included burial pits, landfills, reinjection, chemical stabilization/solidification, and thermal treatments (incineration, thermal desorption), with more recent additions of bioremediation</cite>. <cite id="7750b447-0">Contaminated cuttings can be decontaminated and valorized for reuse in civil construction or repurposed as adsorbents/catalysts for pollutant removal in environmental applications</cite>.

Rock fragments arise not only in oil and gas drilling but also in scientific core drilling (ROV/vibrocoring), mining, and polar geology. <cite id="c56cbe8d-1">ROV-based rock drills and vibrocorers retrieve cores up to 5–6 m in hard rock or soft sediments with water depths up to 2000–6000 m, emphasizing orientation and high-quality sample recovery</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">In ICDP coring operations, a solids-removal/recycling unit recycles drilling fluid and returns cuttings and fluid to the hole, reducing environmental impact and improving cost efficiency</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-4">Wireline coring tools latch and unlatch core barrels to recover ice and rock cores without pulling the entire string, illustrating engineered workflows for rock fragment retrieval and solids handling</cite>.

Valorization addresses material scarcity of high-quality aggregates and binder modifiers, waste-disposal constraints, and environmental risk from hydrocarbons and metals. <cite id="7750b458-1">A holistic review highlights that valorization in civil construction is prominent, with growing use of thermal/chemical pretreatments and a lack of standardized regulation across jurisdictions</cite>.

# Environmental and operational drivers for valorization

Oilfield drill cuttings can leach hydrocarbons and heavy metals, prompting ecological risk and cleanup burdens. <cite id="7750b458-1">Environmental risks include toxicity, bioaccumulation, and contamination by hydrocarbons and heavy metals; characterization and risk assessment are needed to guide reuse</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-4">Bioremediation and other treatments are being applied to reduce contamination before reuse or disposal</cite>. In scientific and mining drilling, solids-control systems recycle cuttings and mud to protect water columns and reduce waste. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">A Heli-Portable Solids Removal Unit recycles drilling fluid and reintroduces cleaned fluid to the borehole, and variable drilling-fluid programs with LCM manage losses while returning cuttings to the drill floor for reuse</cite>.

Marine operations also consider dispersants and site-specific risk. <cite id="7750b458-1">Contaminated cuttings pose marine contamination risks; integrated strategies combining treatment, reuse, and risk assessment are urged to mitigate offshore pollution</cite>.

# Construction and civil-engineering valorization

Concrete and cement-based products offer scalable reuse, with performance that improves with appropriate treatment and blending.

- As cement replacement or mineral additive:
  <cite id="68b61b20-0">Replacing 5–35% cement with drill cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, 22%, and 63% in tests directly comparing specimens; however, replacing 10–20% cement with drill cuttings showed no significant effect on compressive strength, suggesting 20% cement replacement as an optimum in that study</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-3">Replacing 5% cement with dried cuttings reduced compressive strength by 10%, while 10–20% replacements reduced strength by 20%, with significant improvements when additives like fly ash and silica fume were included</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-4">These additives significantly influenced the compressive strength of mixes with 20% drill cuttings</cite>.

- As treated aggregates or fillers:
  <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings at 5–20% replacement (w/b = 0.5; mix 1:1.5:3) achieved 26.2–22.5 N/mm² at 28 days, exceeding minimums for C/20–C/25; 28-day strength activity indices of 90.6–77.6% surpassed the 75% code minimum; wet/dry durability and leachability (chlorides and TPAHs) met reuse targets; pozzolanic activation at 500°C for 180 min improved performance</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Literature reports high compressive strength when drill cuttings form 50–80% of a base course aggregate, and mixes with 20% cement+80% cuttings show stable strength; partially substituting 10–20% sand with cuttings in bricks and concrete produced technically adequate building materials</cite>.

- Design guidance:
  <cite id="68b61b20-0">Incorporating drill cuttings as a partial cement replacement can lower costs, but strength loss grows sharply at higher substitution ratios; 20% cement replacement emerged as a practical upper bound without significant loss in that study</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Pozzolanic activation and optimized w/b (~0.5) mitigate strength reduction and improve durability and leachability compliance</cite>.

Beyond concrete, oilfield cuttings and rock fines can be used as aggregate or filler in bricks, pavers, and blocks, and as raw material for cinder blocks and paving slabs. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Drill cuttings have been used as filler or binder in bricks and concrete, and as aggregate for road bases, with stable strength properties at high inclusion levels</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Using drill cuttings as filler replacement yields lower-grade concrete suitable for foundation blinding, walling, and fill, while additives like fly ash/silica fume can upgrade properties</cite>.

Asphalt and bitumen-modified mixes offer another avenue, leveraging hydrocarbons and filler characteristics.

- Bitumen modification and aggregate replacement:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-2">Asphalt (bitumen) binder protects and binds aggregates; additives/modifiers are used to improve adhesion, reduce mixing/compaction temperatures, and increase resistance to cracking and rutting</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-3">Adding 15% granulated rubber stiffens the binder (penetration shifts from 50/70 to 35/50) and improves temperature susceptibility; rubber addition increases the penetration index, lowers phase angle, and improves elastic properties, confirming better resistance to temperature susceptibility</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Two large-tonnage wastes suitable for asphalt concrete are drill cuttings (containing rock plus up to ~5% oil) and plastics; the oil provides light hydrocarbons that increase bitumen adhesion and reduce aging rate, and cuttings can be used as mineral powder or for paving slabs, curbs, cinder blocks, road components, and organo-mineral mixtures</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-1">Crumb rubber is commonly incorporated by dry-mixing with aggregates for 2-minute blending followed by Marshall compaction, illustrating practical integration of hydrocarbon-rich fillers into binders and mixes</cite>.

- Practical implications:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Because drill cuttings contain oil and angular rock particles, they can act both as a mineral powder and as a source of hydrocarbons that enhance adhesion and slow aging in bitumen; preliminary assessments suggest feasibility as an aggregate or filler with cost reductions and reduced accumulation</cite>.

# Environmental applications: adsorbents, soil conditioners, and catalysts

Contaminated drill cuttings can be decontaminated and repurposed for environmental remediation.

- Adsorbents and catalyst supports:
  <cite id="7750b458-0">Decontaminated drill cuttings have been used as adsorbents and catalysts for pollutant removal from wastewater, and global-scale treatment/valorization solutions have been proposed</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Valorization routes in civil construction and environmental applications are explored in recent reviews, with patent analyses showing growth in thermal/chemical pretreatments that enable reuse</cite>.

- Soil and land uses:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Drill cuttings can be formed into soil-agrarian mixtures and used as components in organo-mineral mixtures for construction and agriculture, leveraging oil content to improve adhesion and reduce aging</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">Bricks and permeable bricks with 10–20% cuttings substitution are technically adequate for building construction, indicating potential for landscaping and non-load-bearing applications</cite>.

These applications benefit from pre-treatment (e.g., thermal activation) to enhance pozzolanicity or surface area and to reduce leachability of contaminants. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Activation at 500°C for 180 minutes improved pozzolanic activity and enabled up to 20% cement replacement without significant strength loss while meeting leachability targets</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Risk assessments and treatment technologies are emphasized to ensure environmental acceptability</cite>.

# Industrial and energy-sector valorization

- Oil/bitumen binder recovery and modification:
  <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Drill cuttings contain up to ~5% oil, which can serve as light hydrocarbon adhesion promoters in bitumen, reducing aging and improving performance in asphalt concrete and related products</cite>.

- Drilling fluid solids control and reintegration:
  <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Mining and scientific coring use solids removal units to return cleaned drilling fluid to the hole and recycle cuttings, reducing environmental footprint and material waste</cite>. In oil and gas, hydrocyclones, centrifuges, and desanders separate reusable solids from mud, enabling re-use of filtrate and return of clean cuttings to the hole or to aggregates processing lines, depending on specifications. <cite id="7750b458-4">Solidification/stabilization and thermal desorption are used to condition cuttings for safe reuse or disposal, and bioremediation has been successfully applied</cite>.

- Backfill and structural fill:
  <cite id="68b61b20-2">Mixtures with 20% cement and 80% drill cuttings demonstrated stable strength properties suitable for road construction, indicating applicability to base/stabilized fills and low-to-medium load bases</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">Filler-grade applications can be supported by additives like fly ash to offset strength loss at higher cuttings fractions</cite>.

# Scientific and geotechnical rock fragment valorization

Scientific coring produces oriented rock cores that can be used for structural, geochemical, and material studies, and the cuttings can be returned to the environment or processed for specific uses. <cite id="c56cbe8d-0">An ROV-based coring tool with an inner non-rotating pipe and chip marks produces oriented cores in soft rocks like limestone, enabling detailed structural analysis</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-2">TV-guided vibrocoring with multiple core barrels (e.g., 10 cm diameter, 50 cm depth) yields high-quality crustal rock samples used for geological and physical property characterization</cite>.

These systems emphasize low-impact operations and solids handling that support reuse. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Recycling units and LCM programs return cuttings and fluid to the hole, reducing environmental impact; solids-control strategies are tailored to borehole conditions</cite>. In permafrost and polar drilling, specialized coring tools and fluid management prevent thermal instability and enable material recovery for construction or environmental management. <cite id="c56cbe8d-4">Ice/rock core recovery tools latch core barrels and circulate drilling fluid, facilitating retrieval without pulling the entire string; this workflow yields intact rock fragments for subsequent reuse</cite>.

# Circular-economy strategies, barriers, and regulatory context

Integrated management is key. <cite id="7750b458-1">A holistic strategy combining characterization, risk assessment, treatment, and legal alignment is needed; reviews emphasize the scarcity of integrated approaches and growing use of thermal/chemical processes, alongside heterogeneous national regulations</cite>.

Technical barriers include variability in composition, contamination, and durability concerns. <cite id="7750b458-1">Drill cuttings vary by formation and fluid chemistry, carrying hydrocarbons and metals that require risk-based management to protect ecosystems and human health</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Strength retention and leachability constraints typically allow up to 20% cement replacement with treated cuttings for structural concrete; beyond this, additives or treatment are required</cite>.

Process and quality control are critical. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Using drill cuttings in asphalt concrete as mineral powder or reinforcing/bitumen modifier requires preliminary assessment of particle size and properties to ensure compatibility and performance</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Operational strategies (HP-SRU, LCM, variable fluid programs) control loss circulation and solids handling, enabling reuse of cuttings and fluid</cite>.

Economic and market barriers include certification, standards, and supply chain integration. <cite id="7750b458-1">Legal/regulatory comparisons reveal a lack of standardized norms for reuse across jurisdictions, which complicates large-scale valorization</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-0">Despite innovation, integrated reviews note the need to link drilling technical complexity with quantitative characterization and reuse pathways</cite>.

# Practical roadmap and examples

- Pre-treatment and qualification:
  <cite id="68b61b20-1">Screening for hydrocarbon and metal leachates; thermal/chemical activation (e.g., 500°C/180 min) to enhance pozzolanicity and durability; target 28-day strength activity indices ≥75–90% for structural uses</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-1">Risk assessment and environmental characterization should precede reuse, with compliance to disposal and reuse regulations</cite>.

- Construction reuse targets:
  - Concrete: <cite id="68b61b20-1">Use treated drill cuttings at 5–20% as cement replacement with w/b ~0.5; 20% is often an upper bound without significant strength loss when additives like fly ash are used</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">At 20% cement replacement, strength may decrease by ~20%, but cost and embodied carbon can be reduced</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">For base course and non-structural uses, 50–80% cuttings in aggregate mixes can yield adequate compressive strength</cite>.
  - Asphalt: <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Use cuttings as mineral powder or integrate oil-rich fines to improve bitumen adhesion and resistance to aging; preliminary tests suggest feasibility with performance comparable to conventional mixes when particle size is controlled</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-3">Rubber-modified binders demonstrate improved temperature susceptibility and elastic properties, illustrating the broader class of hydrocarbon-modified fillers</cite>.

- Environmental reuse:
  <cite id="7750b458-0">After decontamination, drill cuttings can serve as adsorbents/catalysts for wastewater treatment; pilot and case-study programs have demonstrated scalability</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-2">For bricks and permeable pavers, 10–20% cuttings substitution is technically adequate for building applications, expanding market reach</cite>.

- Scientific/industrial integration:
  <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Adopt solids-removal/recycling systems to return clean cuttings and mud to operations, reducing environmental impact and enabling reuse as aggregates or fillers on site</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-1">For ROV/coring programs, co-produce oriented cores for research and manage cuttings with vibrocorers to enable reuse in construction or environmental applications</cite>.

# Key takeaways and remaining gaps

Valorization pathways exist across construction, environmental remediation, and industrial recovery, with demonstrated performance in concrete and asphalt when materials are characterized and treated appropriately. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings can replace up to 20% of cement in structural concrete while meeting strength and durability criteria, provided w/b and activation are optimized</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Oil-bearing drill cuttings can improve bitumen adhesion and reduce aging when used as modifiers or mineral powder in asphalt concrete</cite>. <cite id="7750b458-0">Decontaminated cuttings can be deployed as adsorbents and catalysts for pollution control</cite>. <cite id="c56cbe8d-3">Solids-control integration in mining and marine drilling enables closed-loop reuse of cuttings and mud</cite>.

Critical gaps to resolve at scale include standardized pre-treatment protocols, durable long-term performance data for structural uses, and harmonized regulatory frameworks. <cite id="7750b458-1">Reviews emphasize the scarcity of integrated strategies and regulatory standardization, calling for combined treatment–reuse approaches and risk assessments</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Field-scale durability and environmental leachability monitoring are needed beyond lab curing to validate lifetimes</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-0">Economic valuation studies that compare lifecycle costs of disposal versus valorized products (including carbon and energy footprints) would strengthen adoption</cite>.

In practice, a site-specific valorization plan should combine solids control, decontamination/activation, product design (e.g., 5–20% cement or binder replacement), and compliance with environmental and civil-engineering standards, while leveraging the inherent properties of drill cuttings/rock fragments (angular interlock, mineralogy, and hydrocarbon content) to create circular value. <cite id="7750b458-1">Integrated strategies that align treatment, reuse, and regulation are central to sustainable management</cite>. <cite id="68b61b20-1">Treated drill cuttings have shown adequate structural performance and leachability compliance at 5–20% replacement, with activation improving activity indices</cite>. <cite id="cc08ff45-4">Oil content in cuttings can be harnessed to improve bitumen performance in asphalt mixes, expanding reuse horizons</cite>.

Title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
Snippet: The decontaminated drill cutting can be used in civil construction or can be repurposed in the environmental sector as adsorbents or catalysts for removing pollutants from wastewater (Yang et al. 2022a). Additionally, there is an opportunity to implement global-scale treatment and valorization solutions for drill cuttings contaminated (de Almeida et al. 2017;Cherepovitsyn and Lebedev 2023). 

Although prior studies have addressed specific aspects of drilling waste management, there is a notable scarcity of integrated reviews that link the technical complexities of drilling with the quantitative characterization and valorization of drill cuttings. This article aims to address this knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive view, from waste generation to potential reuse. This review is organized into the following topics: (1) Types of oil well drilling; (2) Drilling fluids; (3) Toxicity of drilling fluids; (4) Characterization methods of drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids; (5) Risk assessment; (6) Treatment technologies for drill cuttings management; (7) Valorization of drill cuttings; (8) Case studies and pilot-scale trials (9) Innovative advances in treatment; and (9) Legal aspects. This work is of particular importance in stimulating discussion and providing a foundational reference for those developing or implementing strategies for drill cutting management, thereby supporting more sustainable practices in the oil industry.

Title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
Snippet: The construction of offshore oil and gas wells, especially during the drilling phase, generates a large volume of waste, particularly drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids, which represent a source of marine environmental contamination. Despite research on the environmental impacts of fluid-contaminated drill cuttings, there is still a scarcity of review articles on the topic from a holistic perspective. Therefore, this article presents a critical review of the generation, characterization, environmental impacts, treatment, valorization by reusing, and final disposal regulations for drill cuttings. Drilling methods and the fluids used are discussed, along with associated environmental risks, such as toxicity, bioaccumulation, and contamination by heavy metals and petroleum hydrocarbons. Methodologies for characterization and risk assessment are addressed, with an emphasis on the geographical limitation of studies and the absence of regionalized models. The potential for valorization of drill cuttings is explored, primarily in civil construction. Patent analysis reveals a growing trend in the utilization of thermal and chemical processes for drill cutting treatment. From a legal perspective, a regulatory comparison among countries highlights the lack of normative standardization. Overall, the sustainable management of drill cuttings requires integrated strategies that combine effective treatment, valorization by reusing, and risk assessments. Accordingly, this study could contribute to the development of sustainable drill cuttings management strategies, which would mitigate marine pollution and promote more environmentally responsible practices within the oil industry.

Title: A review of the current options for the treatment and safe disposal of drill cuttings
Snippet: Drilling for the exploration and extraction of oil requires the use of drilling fluids which are continuously pumped down and returned carrying the rock phase that is extracted from the well. The potential environmental impacts of contaminated fluids from drilling operations have attracted increasing community awareness and scrutiny. This review article highlights current advances in the treatment of drill cuttings and compares the technologies in terms of cost, time and space requirements. Traditionally, a range of non-biological methods have been employed for the disposal of drill cuttings including burial pits, landfills and re-injection, chemical stabilization and solidification and thermal treatments such as incineration and thermal desorption. More recently, bioremediation has been successfully applied as a treatment process for cuttings. This review provides a current comparison of bioremediation technologies and non-biological technologies for the treatment of contaminated drill cuttings providing information on a number of factors that need to be taken into account when choosing the best technology for drilling waste management including the environmental risks associated with disposal of drilling wastes.

Title: Feasibility Study of the Potential Use of Drill Cuttings in Concrete
Snippet: This study assesses the feasibility of using drill cuttings in concrete as a partial replacement of cement. The following conclusions have been drawn from this study:  Drill cuttings can be used as a partial replacement with cement in concrete. Results indicated that compare to control sample, the specimens containing 5%, 20%, and 35% of drill cutting showed 10%, 22%, and 63% reduction in their compressive strength. It was also found that replacing 10, 15, and 20% of cement with drill cutting do not have a significant effect on the compressive strength of prepared samples. Therefore, replacing 20% of cement with drilling waste was considered as the optimum value.  It has been found that flyash is of particular value in high-strength concrete. Therefore, various percentage of flyash including 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25% were added to concrete samples containing 20% drill cuttings. Results showed that the compressive strength of the concrete samples with 15-20% flyash was increased by 33%. However, adding 25% of flyash significantly reduces their compressive strength.

Title: Compressive strength and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production
Snippet: This study examines the compressive strengths and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production. Workability tests on various water-binder ratios (w/b) on the fresh concrete showed that an optimum w/b of 0.5 was adequate for the concrete to be workable. Replacement levels of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25% were used to produce cement-drill cuttings concrete at a 1:1.5:3 mix ratio. The blended concrete gave a compressive strength in the range of 26.20N/mm 2 for 5% to 22.46N/mm 2 for 20% replacement levels at 28 days curing time, more than the minimum compressive strength of 20N/mm 2 and 25N/mm 2 specified for concrete strength class C/20 and C/25, respectively. The strength activity index of 90.56, 98.76, 89.05, 98.05, and 77.64% for 5, 10, 15, and 20% replacement levels at 28 days of curing time was obtained surpassing the minimum 75% specified for normal concrete by the code. The wet/dry durability effects of the blended concrete at any replacement level passed the structural integrity with less than 5% of the structural integrity of the material lost. The chloride and total polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (TPAHs) leachability effects both met the DPRs target values for reusable materials. The study has shown that drill cuttings have a good pozzolanic effect on concrete, especially when activated at the temperature of 500oC for 180 minutes. It also shows that treated drill cuttings could replace cement up to 20% by weight to produce concrete of adequate strength using a w/b ratio of 0.5 and mix ratios of 1:1.5:3. The study has also shown that treated drill cuttings replaced with cement to produce concrete which is durable to both wet/dry and leaching effects of chlorides and TPAHs to the environment.

Title: Comparative evaluation of the compressive strength of treated drill cutting blocks and sandcrete blocks
Snippet: Drill cuttings have been found to retain high compressive strength, when incorporated as an aggregate in concrete production (6). A high compressive material suitable for use in pavement bases construction was obtained when drill cuttings of about 50% to 80% was incorporated in the material mix (7). The findings from (8)study reveal that a mixture containing 20% cement and 80% drill cuttings demonstrates stable strength properties, making it appropriate for use in road construction. Similarly, (9) found the compressive strength of bricks, concrete mix and permeable bricks; partially substituted sand with (10% and 20%) of drill cuttings is technically adequate for use in building construction. 

However, the study by (10) suggests that substituting 5% of cement with drill cutting in concrete production reduces the compressive strength of the concrete by 20%, while incorporating additives such as fly ash and silica fume will significantly improve th ecompressive strenght of the concrete.Thus using drill cuutings as filler replacement produces concrete with lower strenght grade that can be apply in foundation blinding, walling and concrete fill material (11). Recent and past studies on drill cutting application focused on the partial incorporation in concrete mix or use as a filler or binder in building construction.

Title: Feasibility Study of the Potential Use of Drill Cuttings in Concrete
Snippet: Abstract Increasing the need of energy and its high price tempts companies to drill more oil wells every day and create more drilling waste. Most of these drilling wastes are managed to be disposed but they will always have many environmental impacts. Therefore, this study investigates the potential of using drill cuttings in concrete as a partial replacement of cement. The innovation of this study is not only to produce a new and cost-effective material from drill cuttings, but also to mitigate its negative environmental impacts. To achieve this objective, laboratory studies carried out to quantify the compressive strength of concrete samples and to determine the chemical composition of drill cuttings. Results showed that replacing 5% of cement with dried drill cuttings reduces the compressive strength of concrete by 10%. However, comprehensive strength of concrete samples decreases by 20% when replacing 10, 15, and 20% of cement with drill cuttings. Furthermore, the effect of some additives such as fly ash and silica fume on the compressive strength of the concrete samples containing drill cuttings was studied. It was concluded that adding these additives have a significant influence on the compressive strength of concrete samples containing 20% drill cuttings.

documents.title: Feasibility Study of the Potential Use of Drill Cuttings in Concrete
documents.snippet: This study assesses the feasibility of using drill cuttings in concrete as a partial replacement of cement. The following conclusions have been drawn from this study:  Drill cuttings can be used as a partial replacement with cement in concrete. Results indicated that compare to control sample, the specimens containing 5%, 20%, and 35% of drill cutting showed 10%, 22%, and 63% reduction in their compressive strength. It was also found that replacing 10, 15, and 20% of cement with drill cutting do not have a significant effect on the compressive strength of prepared samples. Therefore, replacing 20% of cement with drilling waste was considered as the optimum value.  It has been found that flyash is of particular value in high-strength concrete. Therefore, various percentage of flyash including 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25% were added to concrete samples containing 20% drill cuttings. Results showed that the compressive strength of the concrete samples with 15-20% flyash was increased by 33%. However, adding 25% of flyash significantly reduces their compressive strength.

documents.title: Compressive strength and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production
documents.snippet: This study examines the compressive strengths and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production. Workability tests on various water-binder ratios (w/b) on the fresh concrete showed that an optimum w/b of 0.5 was adequate for the concrete to be workable. Replacement levels of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25% were used to produce cement-drill cuttings concrete at a 1:1.5:3 mix ratio. The blended concrete gave a compressive strength in the range of 26.20N/mm 2 for 5% to 22.46N/mm 2 for 20% replacement levels at 28 days curing time, more than the minimum compressive strength of 20N/mm 2 and 25N/mm 2 specified for concrete strength class C/20 and C/25, respectively. The strength activity index of 90.56, 98.76, 89.05, 98.05, and 77.64% for 5, 10, 15, and 20% replacement levels at 28 days of curing time was obtained surpassing the minimum 75% specified for normal concrete by the code. The wet/dry durability effects of the blended concrete at any replacement level passed the structural integrity with less than 5% of the structural integrity of the material lost. The chloride and total polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (TPAHs) leachability effects both met the DPRs target values for reusable materials. The study has shown that drill cuttings have a good pozzolanic effect on concrete, especially when activated at the temperature of 500oC for 180 minutes. It also shows that treated drill cuttings could replace cement up to 20% by weight to produce concrete of adequate strength using a w/b ratio of 0.5 and mix ratios of 1:1.5:3. The study has also shown that treated drill cuttings replaced with cement to produce concrete which is durable to both wet/dry and leaching effects of chlorides and TPAHs to the environment.

Title: Rotation of the Philippine Sea plate inferred from paleomagnetism of oriented cores taken with an ROV-based coring apparatus
Snippet: An ROV-based coring apparatus recently developed by KOKEN BORING MACHINE CO. LED. was used for taking oriented cores from the seafloor (Fig. 2a). The maximum penetration length is 37 cm, which enables to drill target rocks covered with relatively thick manganese (Mn) crust. The core diameter is 3 cm. The drilling rod consists of an inner pipe and an outer pipe with a drill bit (Fig. 2b). The inner pipe does not rotate, which enables coring of soft rocks such as limestone. The inside of the inner pipe is not straight but slightly inclined at a certain point of the pipe to snap off a core from bedrock. The inner pipe has a hard chip at its entrance to mark an orientation line to a core (Fig. 2d). The direction and inclination of the orientation line are measured with a sensor unit (a magnetic compass and inclinometer) placed on the frame of the corer. Using this technique, we can obtain fully oriented cores such as those used for onshore paleomagnetic research. Refer Tajima et al. (2020) for more information of the coring apparatus.

Title: British geological survey remotely operated sea bed rockdrills and vibrocorers: new advances to meet the needs of the scientific community
Snippet: The British Geological Survey (BGS) built their first remotely operated rock drill in the late 1960s. CONSUB (Fig. 1) was a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) capable of retrieving short cores from the seabed. It was decommissioned in the early 1970s to be replaced by the midi-drill. The midi-drill (1975The midi-drill ( -1983 was capable of acquiring cores up to 1m long and was constrained to shallower water depths. As scientific exploration moved into deeper water a new version of the rock drill (RD1) was designed and built in-house (Fig. 2). RD1 is a combined rockdrill and vibrocoring system offering the flexibility of two sampling systems in one rig to the scientific and commercial communities. RD1 is capable of retrieving cores up to 5m long in "hard rock" via traditional rotary coring techniques and cores up to 6m long in "soft sediment" environments in vibrocorer mode. The maximum operational water depth for the RD1 system is 2000m. The RD1 system has been operational since 1982 and is still in use today. The Oriented Drill was specifically designed to recover samples for use in palaeomagnetic studies and was initially developed for use on the Natural Environment Research Council (NERC) funded BRIDGE Programme (British Mid-Ocean Ridge Programme;1996-1998 on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. The maximum core length is 0.8m and the maximum operational water depth of the drill is 5500m. Orientation is achieved by scribing the core along its length with a single reference line and then using the two drill-mounted compasses to assign a heading to this reference mark. This mark can then be related to a world reference thereby facilitating detailed palaeomagnetic analysis.

The BGS have designed, built and operated vibrocorers since the 1970s and are the BGS's oldest form of powered coring device with a long and successful track record of recovering high-quality samples worldwide from Greenland to the Scottish fjords. The system can be configured for 3m, 4m or 6m maximum core lengths and can operate in maximum water depths of 2000m via the BGS umbilical winch or 6000m water depth using the new battery-operated system (Fig. 3).

Title: Geological characterization and controlling factors of small-scale variations in the cobalt-rich ferromanganese crust deposits
Snippet: Rock sampling was performed using a BMS (NiGK Corporation, Japan) with a TV camera at the bottom, observing the seafloor, and drilling two to four cores per site where the CRC are exposed. The BMS contained up to 12 core barrels with plastic tubes inside, with a core diameter of 10 cm and a maximum drilling depth of 50 cm below the sea floor. The acquired drilled samples were recovered on board, water-cleaned, and split in half with a diamond saw. Cross sections were photographed, and geological and physical properties were described.

Title: Expedition 364 methods
Snippet: The coring rig utilized was the International Continental Scientific Drilling Project (ICDP) Atlas Copco T3WDH mining rig, utilizing flush-jointed mining drill strings and a modified top drive. The rig had a mast capable of handling 6 m string lengths, and coring was conducted using a specially built coring top drive system installed in the mast (Figure F6). Wireline operation of the core barrel was conducted through broken, locked drill string. The coring rig was cantilevered off the bow of the L/B Myrtle (Figure F4). The drilling and coring plan was carefully designed to allow the greatest number of options for casing, drill rod/barrel, and core diameters. 

An AMC Heli-Portable Solids Removal Unit (HP-SRU) was utilized to reduce the environmental impact and cost efficiency of the hole through a drilling fluid recycling system. Cuttings and drilling fluid were returned to the drill floor once open-hole drilling commenced. The drilling fluid was cleaned and filtered within the HP-SRU. The cleaned drilling fluid was added to a batch of newly mixed drilling fluid before being returned to the borehole. At 79 m DSF, drilling fluid did not return to the drill floor due to a loss of circulation. Below this depth, the remainder of the open-hole interval was drilled using seawater, with the occasional addition of drilling mud to reduce friction. 

The HP-SRU was also used in the cored interval. A variable drilling fluid program comprising combinations of seawater, mud products, and loss circulation material (LCM) was used, depending on borehole conditions. Several zones of lost circulation were encountered. Goff et al., (2016). Regional bathymetry from Amante et al., (2009).

Title: Agile Sub-Ice Geological (ASIG) Drill development and Pirrit Hills field project
Snippet: Tanner Kuhl and others surface of the reamers includes diamond-impregnated surfaces with zero borehole clearance separated by waterways for drilling fluid circulation. The TK56 wireline coring tools allow a core barrel assembly to be alternately latched and unlatched into the BHA to recover ice and rock core to the surface without having to pull the entire drill string every run (Fig. 7a). The core barrel assembly is pumped down with normal circulating drill fluid to the BHA, where it automatically latches into the outer core barrel (Fig. 7b). An optional dry-hole lowering device can be used to trip the inner core barrel assembly to the bottom using the wireline winch. The bottom of the inner core barrel, which sits directly behind  the coring bit face when latched into the outer core barrel, contains a split-ring tapered core lifter that grips the core (ice and rock) when the drill string is lifted slightly during core break and retains the core in the inner core barrel. The wireline winch is used in conjunction with an overshot to connect to the core barrel head assembly at the top of the inner core barrel, unlatch the head assembly from the outer core barrel and pull the core barrel assembly to the surface. Core barrels are available for 1.5 and 3 m core lengths. 

Several fishing tools are available to help retrieve broken tooling from the borehole. Tapered recovery taps with sharp, righthand threads are available for both drill pipe and casing. They are run downhole on drill pipe and rotated to thread into the top of broken or dropped pipe/casing for retrieval. An expanding recovery tap can also be used for recovering drill pipe without rotation. A casing cutter is included with ASIG for cutting off stuck casing that cannot be otherwise retrieved. It is run downhole on drill pipe and features a milling cutter that expands   Drilling fluid can be removed from a borehole with a swab assembly or with a bailer. The swab assembly runs on the wireline winch inside the drill pipe string.
