Title: Identification of mechanical and techno-economic impacts of recycled brick demolition waste in paving block production
Snippet: The techno-economic analysis method for the process of reusing brick wall demolition waste into paving blocks begins by calculating all costs, from waste collection to paving block molding. 

The following is a description of the techno-economic analysis process in this study: a) the price of cement is determined by the current market rates per kilogram; b) the price of natural sand is an example of the conventional cost of fine aggregate; c) the cost of recycling from brick demolition, including material preparation, screening, and crushing; d) labor expenses for the processes of mixing, molding, and curing; e) energy expenditure related to the operation of machines during compaction and crushing; f) the cost of transportation, which takes into consideration the transportation of raw materials from their source locations to the production site; g) the combination of these components represents the total cost of producing paving blocks using recycled and natural aggregates. 

The following is a comparative analysis of the technical and economic uses of the two materials: a) cost per unit, measured in square meters of finished paving blocks (IDR/block); b) cost savings (%), which is the percentage reduction in production costs when recycled brick waste is used instead of natural sand; c) resource efficiency, which represents the financial and environmental benefits of using recycled aggregates, is calculated as the percentage reduction in natural sand use. 

The economic feasibility of this study is based on a direct comparison of performance with consistent live applications. This value is based on: a) energy, cement, and natural sand were used based on local market prices in the area; b) production capacity is expected to be consistent with small-scale paving block manufacturing conditions, where molding, drying, and mixing are performed by hand or with light mechanical equipment; c) to avoid performance bias between recycled aggregate and natural sand combinations, technical limitations and assumptions include fixed mix proportions for all cost comparisons, comparable drying conditions, and equivalent specimen sizes; d) these boundary conditions define the economic environment of the analysis and ensure that the comparison accurately reflects typical production conditions in Asia.

Title: Physical and Mechanical Properties of Concrete using Recycled Clay Bricks as Coarse Aggregate
Snippet: This only suggests that more brick waste will be generated over the years and appropriate recycling methods should be explored. 

Bricks are considered waste if they break during production, or they are collected from construction and demolition sites (Demir and Orhan, 2003;Sadek, 2012). Recycling such bricks would solve an important issue and reduce the strain on landfills (Lennon, 2005). Also, recycling could prove to be a cheaper alternative to landfilling; for example, it has been reported that reprocessing one ton of bricks, blocks, and concrete would cost about $21 per ton; while landfilling, on the other hand, would cost a staggering $136 per ton in comparison (Lennon, 2005). Reusing bricks in the fabrication of concrete can moderate the demand for NCA (Abed et al., 2020;Adamson et al., 2015) and solve the problem of dealing with construction waste (Leite and Santana, 2019). Moreover, due to their lighter weight compared to NCA, the use of bricks can help produce lightweight concrete, which ultimately results in savings in energy and cost due to lower self-weight (Al-shannag and Charif, 2017). 

Recycled bricks have been used previously as base filler in roads (Etxeberria et al., 2007a) and the lack of understanding of the behavior of concrete made with bricks has limited their use in the past (Debieb and Kenai, 2008). Previous studies have shown that crushed bricks have the potential to act as aggregates to form ordinary concrete (Dang and Zhao, 2019;Hoque et al., 2020) and due to their lower specific gravity in comparison to NCA, greater replacement of the latter by Crushed Brick Aggregates (CBA) causes a reduction in density. For example, an up to 18% reduction in density was observed at 30% CBA replacement of NCA (Alwash and Al-Khafaji, 2018). 

Furthermore, several studies have reported that the replacement of NCA with CBA causes a 10-35% fall in the compressive strength when coarse aggregates are substituted and 30-40% when fine aggregates are replaced (Debieb and Kenai, 2008;Khalaf and Devenny, 2005;Noaman et al., 2021).

Title: Environmental savings from concrete reuse: examining the limitations and optimal practices for cutting thresholds of concrete building components for reuse
Snippet: Our study examined the GHG emissions of reusing concrete in construction compared to the traditional approach of producing and transporting new concrete. By analysing the GHG emissions associated with preparing reused concrete, we found that concrete reuse could offer significant environmental advantages as long as it is carefully considered. Specifically, the extent of these environmental benefits varies based on several factors, including the cutting size, transportation distance, cutting tool efficiency, and energy consumption rate of the cutting equipment. snippet.text:
The techno-economic analysis method for the process of reusing brick wall demolition waste into paving blocks begins by calculating all costs, from waste collection to paving block molding. 

The following is a description of the techno-economic analysis process in this study: a) the price of cement is determined by the current market rates per kilogram; b) the price of natural sand is an example of the conventional cost of fine aggregate; c) the cost of recycling from brick demolition, including material preparation, screening, and crushing; d) labor expenses for the processes of mixing, molding, and curing; e) energy expenditure related to the operation of machines during compaction and crushing; f) the cost of transportation, which takes into consideration the transportation of raw materials from their source locations to the production site; g) the combination of these components represents the total cost of producing paving blocks using recycled and natural aggregates. 

The following is a comparative analysis of the technical and economic uses of the two materials: a) cost per unit, measured in square meters of finished paving blocks (IDR/block); b) cost savings (%), which is the percentage reduction in production costs when recycled brick waste is used instead of natural sand; c) resource efficiency, which represents the financial and environmental benefits of using recycled aggregates, is calculated as the percentage reduction in natural sand use. 

The economic feasibility of this study is based on a direct comparison of performance with consistent live applications. This value is based on: a) energy, cement, and natural sand were used based on local market prices in the area; b) production capacity is expected to be consistent with small-scale paving block manufacturing conditions, where molding, drying, and mixing are performed by hand or with light mechanical equipment; c) to avoid performance bias between recycled aggregate and natural sand combinations, technical limitations and assumptions include fixed mix proportions for all cost comparisons, comparable drying conditions, and equivalent specimen sizes; d) these boundary conditions define the economic environment of the analysis and ensure that the comparison accurately reflects typical production conditions in Asia.

This only suggests that more brick waste will be generated over the years and appropriate recycling methods should be explored. 

Bricks are considered waste if they break during production, or they are collected from construction and demolition sites (Demir and Orhan, 2003;Sadek, 2012). Recycling such bricks would solve an important issue and reduce the strain on landfills (Lennon, 2005). Also, recycling could prove to be a cheaper alternative to landfilling; for example, it has been reported that reprocessing one ton of bricks, blocks, and concrete would cost about $21 per ton; while landfilling, on the other hand, would cost a staggering $136 per ton in comparison (Lennon, 2005). Reusing bricks in the fabrication of concrete can moderate the demand for NCA (Abed et al., 2020;Adamson et al., 2015) and solve the problem of dealing with construction waste (Leite and Santana, 2019). Moreover, due to their lighter weight compared to NCA, the use of bricks can help produce lightweight concrete, which ultimately results in savings in energy and cost due to lower self-weight (Al-shannag and Charif, 2017). 

Recycled bricks have been used previously as base filler in roads (Etxeberria et al., 2007a) and the lack of understanding of the behavior of concrete made with bricks has limited their use in the past (Debieb and Kenai, 2008). Previous studies have shown that crushed bricks have the potential to act as aggregates to form ordinary concrete (Dang and Zhao, 2019;Hoque et al., 2020) and due to their lower specific gravity in comparison to NCA, greater replacement of the latter by Crushed Brick Aggregates (CBA) causes a reduction in density. For example, an up to 18% reduction in density was observed at 30% CBA replacement of NCA (Alwash and Al-Khafaji, 2018). 

Furthermore, several studies have reported that the replacement of NCA with CBA causes a 10-35% fall in the compressive strength when coarse aggregates are substituted and 30-40% when fine aggregates are replaced (Debieb and Kenai, 2008;Khalaf and Devenny, 2005;Noaman et al., 2021).

judgment.criterion_reasoning: The answer explicitly acknowledges throughout that most valorization studies establish technical feasibility without providing comprehensive comparative lifecycle assessments. Key passages include: 'Life-cycle comparisons show trade-offs among options (e.g., onshore solidification vs reinjection), with different pollutant emissions profiles and needs for better environmental assessment' [2]; 'Which option has less environmental impact needs further assessment' [2]; 'Trade-offs are context-specific and sensitive to process choices; some LCAs call for further assessment before concluding superiority' (Limitations section); and the core message that 'outcomes are context-dependent and can be inferior if contaminants are not adequately addressed or logistics raise embodied burdens.' The answer does not definitively claim valorization is superior based solely on feasibility studies; instead, it systematically addresses processing energy (thermal desorption, solidification emissions), contaminant risks (heavy metals, hydrocarbons requiring verification), transportation costs (distance optimization effects), and environmental accounting (CO2 vs particulate trade-offs, life-cycle burdens). The answer appropriately qualifies that superiority depends on 'decontamination quality,' 'treatment pathways matched to local regulations,' 'market proximity,' and process optimization, and repeatedly notes that comparative analyses show different burden profiles requiring context-specific evaluation.

Reference [3] is about recycled clay bricks in concrete (not drill cuttings), and while the cost comparison analogy is reasonable, the answer could make clearer that this is an analogous case rather than direct drill cuttings evidence.

Reference [9] is about recycled brick demolition waste in paving blocks, not drill cuttings; while used for techno-economic analysis methodology illustration, the relevance could be stated more explicitly.

A system can retrieve multiple valorization pathways but must recognize that compositional heterogeneity makes any single 'optimal' pathway claim invalid: what works for water-based shale cuttings may be completely inappropriate for oil-contaminated sandstone cuttings. attempts.answer:
Summary
Maximizing resource recovery from drill cuttings and rock fragments requires a context-adaptive, multi-node valorization “superstructure” that first cleans and characterizes the material, then departs into parallel tracks: oil/wax and drilling-fluid solids recovery; hydrometallurgical or physical recovery of base/precious metals and critical elements; and downcycling into construction/industrial feeds (e.g., cement raw meal, graded aggregates). This approach aligns mineralogy, contamination state, and market viability to maximize total value; process windows with demonstrated performance include solvent/thermal decontamination to <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement, supercritical CO2 extraction up to ~49% oil, and hydromet flowsheets (leach → SX/EW or cementation) for Cu/Ni/Zn depending on host phases and drilling fluid chemistry. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Drill cuttings are a heterogeneous, underutilized secondary reservoir for critical elements, and recovery must be mineralogy-guided due to variable REE host phases and drilling-fluid effects</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can be reused in civil construction or deployed as adsorbents/catalysts; integrated reviews emphasize full chains from generation to reuse with case studies and legal aspects</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-2">Rigorous sampling, cleaning, and size separation are needed to avoid cross-contamination and bias in composition</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-3">Offshore cuttings comprise mixed lithologies from sands to limestones; their fine, disaggregated nature complicates analysis and use</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling-mud components (bentonite, barite, carbonates) overlap with mineral grains and must be accounted for; cleaning and per-case correction are recommended</cite>.

1) Why a single, fixed “pathway” fails
Drill cuttings are inherently heterogeneous mixtures of rock fragments, entrained drilling fluid solids, and adsorbed hydrocarbons, with compositions that shift by lithology (carbonates, shales, sandstones), drilling fluid type (water-based vs oil-based), and operational regime (offshore HDD, geothermal, mining). <cite id="3d07b152-3">Offshore sequences produce mixed lithologies (sandstone, siltstone, shale, limestone) in silt-to-fine-sand fractions</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/calcite hematite inputs and casing fragments complicate mineralogy and require cleaning to avoid misattribution</cite>. Their metal content arises from both matrix minerals and drilling-fluid cuttings (e.g., bentonite clays), so recovery strategies must separate entrained solids and account for contamination before any extraction. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Cleaning and sieving protocols reduce cross-contamination and enable representative sampling</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling fluid granulations overlap with mineral grains; improper washing alters mineralogy and composition unpredictably</cite>. A single pathway cannot globally “maximize” recovery; instead, a modular decision framework should route cuttings through pre-treatment, analytics, and parallel recovery trains tuned to host mineralogy and contamination. <cite id="3d07b152-0">A mineral-first framework links REE host phases to distinct leaching pathways and proposes a decision-tree to align mineralogy with extraction methods</cite>.

2) Core unit operations and interfaces
- Characterization and decontamination. Sieving, washing, and mechanical removal of drilling fluid solids (e.g., bentonite, barite) and casing fragments are prerequisites; magnets can remove ferrous fragments, while density/centrifugal separation can target barite and clays. <cite id="3d07b152-2">A 100-mesh sieve and fixed-interval sampling cleaned of mud coatings reduce cross-contamination</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/carbonates are common drilling-fluid inputs overlapping in size; casing fragments can be magnetically removed</cite>. Analytics (pXRF, XRD, SEM/MLA) guide downstream choices and correct for comminution/cleaning effects. <cite id="3d07b152-3">SEM-automated mineralogy reveals mixed lithologies in fine grains</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">pXRF on cuttings requires comminution and correction for cleaning-induced loss of fines</cite>.
- Oil and drilling-fluid oil recovery. Centrifugation, leaching with selective solvents, and thermal routes separate oil and entrained drilling fluid; de-oiled cuttings then qualify for construction reuse. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching with optimized solvent/temperature/time (e.g., 1:3 cutting:solvent ratio, >60 °C for 30 min) efficiently removes oil from oily cuttings to <1% residual, enabling road paving or cement/plaster feed; recyclable solvent and oil can be looped back for reuse</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-1">A novel leaching solvent achieved oil on cuttings below 0.6% with recyclable solvent/oil streams, reducing costs and enabling reuse</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 can extract up to 49% oily fluid at 200 bar; microwave/thermal decontamination reduces oil from 8.03% to 1.87% and can achieve >98% oil recovery at >350 °C and >50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids enable effective separation of drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery for reuse, supporting integrated management to enhance material recovery</cite>.
- Metals and critical elements recovery. Hydrometallurgical flowsheets (acid/alkali leach → separation via solvent extraction, ion exchange, adsorption → electrowinning/cementation) recover Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, and others depending on host and lixiviants; process intensity (temperature, time, oxidants, microwave) tunes extraction kinetics. <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydrometallurgy uses acid/caustic leaching followed by separation (SX, ion exchange, adsorption) and metal recovery via electrorefining/EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy is effective for Cu and can extract Fe, Sn, Zn, Al, Ni, Pb depending on lixiviant and downstream strategy; challenges include long times, acid hazards, heavy metal contamination risks, residues, and wastewater</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching (1–4 M NaOH, 20–80 °C) can extract Pb ~60% in 15 min at 80 °C and Zn ~58% at 4 M NaOH; intensification via oxidants or microwaves increases leaching efficiency</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">Solvent extraction with LIX 984N selectively extracts Cu from sulfate solutions; extraction depends on pH and enables separation of Cu/Ni/Zn</cite> <cite id="602407f5-4">Leaching, SX, and EW are core steps for oxide ores; cementation is a cheaper, less selective alternative to recover copper from pregnant solutions</cite>. Mineralogy-guided leaching is key: organically bound or ion-adsorbed REEs require different chemistries than structurally integrated phosphates, and drilling fluids alter surface chemistry and integrity. <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE occurrence across host phases (ion-adsorbed clays, organically bound, structurally integrated phosphates) dictates distinct leaching pathways; drilling fluids influence surface chemistry and integrity, requiring matched extraction methods</cite>.
- Downcycling to construction/industrial feeds. De-oiled, de-sanded cuttings can be stabilized and used for road base or as raw materials in cement and plaster; pre-treatment to <1% oil and removal of ferrous/casing fragments improves compliance and performance. <cite id="62147b4a-0">After leaching to <1% oil, cuttings can be paved or used as cement/plaster raw materials; recyclable oil and solvent reduce costs and pollution</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated drill cuttings can be reused in civil construction and repurposed as adsorbents/catalysts for wastewater treatment</cite>. For rock fragments from geotechnical drilling (HDD or tunneling), sieving and cleaning enable graded sands/fines for construction or environmental media. <cite id="3d07b152-2">A 100-mesh sieve and careful cleaning of bentonite/polymer residues yield representative, cross-contaminant-reduced cuttings for reuse</cite>.

3) Operation-specific valorization pathways
Offshore oil and gas (rig-based, marine)  
- Pre-treatment and analytics: high-pressure washing, magnetic removal, and density-based barite/bentonite separation; pXRF/XRD to classify lithologies and contamination. <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/carbonates overlap in size with minerals; cleaning/correction is required to avoid misattribution</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-3">Mixed lithologies and comminuted fines complicate use; SEM-MLA informs provenance and mineralogy</cite>.  
- Oil/wax and drilling-fluid recovery: combine solvent leaching and/or microwave/thermal decontamination to produce oil-free cuttings for aggregates/cement while closing-looping oil and drilling fluid. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to 1:3 ratio, >60 °C/30 min, yields <1% oil cuttings for paving/cement; solvent and oil are recyclable</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 extracts up to 49% at 200 bar; microwave/thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% and enable >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids separate drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery, enabling integrated reuse</cite>.  
- Metals recovery: where cuttings contain sulfides/oxides or drilling-derived metal fines (e.g., steel tool fragments), hydromet flowsheets recover ferrous/non-ferrous metals; selective SX/EW for Cu/Ni/Zn and cementation for Pb. <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy effectively recovers Cu and can target Fe, Sn, Zn, Ni, Pb depending on lixiviants and separation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching at 80 °C (1–4 M NaOH) extracts Pb (~60%) and Zn (~58%) rapidly; oxidants/microwaves accelerate kinetics</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">LIX 984N selectively extracts Cu; pH controls selectivity for Cu/Ni/Zn separation</cite>.  
- Side-streams to circular markets: decontaminated fines as adsorbents/catalysts and construction fill; oil recovered can be reprocessed as make-up for drilling fluids. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can serve as adsorbents/catalysts for pollutant removal and as construction fill</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing costs</cite>.

Onshore oil and gas/geothermal/mineral drilling  
- Pre-treatment adapted to formation lithology: carbonate-rich zones benefit from acid leaching to desorb drilling fluid and mobilize fines; clay-rich zones need gentle pH-tuned leaching to avoid dispersion. <cite id="602407f5-2">Leaching conditions (concentration, temperature, time) and porosity control diffusion and efficiency; alkaline leaching efficiently removes Pb/Zn from oxide-like dusts</cite>.  
- Metals focus: where formations host oxide/hydroxide or sulfide minerals (e.g., Cu-bearing carbonates, Ni/Co laterites), hydromet flowsheets recover multiple metals with SX/EW or cementation; REEs in drilling mud-bearing shales require acid/carbonate systems matched to host phases. <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE occurrence governs leaching chemistry; drilling fluids alter surfaces, so extraction must align with host phase and contamination</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">Solvent extraction selectively separates Cu/Ni/Zn from sulfate solutions; pH control is central</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s selectivity and lower energy can extract a broader suite of metals but generates residues and wastewater needing treatment</cite>.  
- Oil and brine valorization: in geothermal brine environments, thermal/membrane separations can decontaminate cuttings and recover heat/beneficiaries; oil recovered supports energy recovery. <cite id="62147b4a-3">Pyrolysis/microwave heating desorb hydrocarbons with product streams recoverable for reuse; solids can proceed to aggregates/cement</cite>.  
- Aggregates and road base: de-oiled cuttings meeting <1% oil pass into stabilization or cement-bound mixes after ensuring absence of drilling fluid fines; careful cleaning prevents long-term performance degradation. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to <1% oil enables road paving or cement/plaster use; solvent/oil recycling improves sustainability</cite>.

High-density directional drilling (HDD) and tunneling  
- Episode-based valorization: collect cuttings with sieves/cyclones; clean polymer/bentonite coatings; size-grade for immediate reuse in backfill or environmental applications, then route de-oiled fractions into cement-bound materials. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Use of 100-mesh sieve and cleaning protocols yields representative, cross-contaminant-reduced cuttings</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can be used for construction and environmental applications</cite>.  
- Metals and REEs in cored fragments: where cores include carbonatite/alkaline complexes, apply mineralogy-driven REE leaching; tool steel fragments are ferrosed by hydromet or magnetically recovered. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided REE extraction across host phases with decision-tree routing</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy recovers multiple metals with established flowsheets</cite>.

4) An integrated, multi-node “superstructure” to maximize total recovery
A robust valorization “superstructure” decouples contaminant removal from element-specific recovery, feeding multiple markets:
- Node A: Decontamination hub (centrifugation, leaching, ionic liquid/supercritical options) to produce oil-free, solids-depleted cuttings for construction reuse, while capturing oil, brine, and entrained drilling solids. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Solvent leaching achieves <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement with solvent and oil recyclability</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 extracts up to 49% oil at 200 bar; thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% with >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids separate drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery</cite>.  
- Node B: Hydrometallurgical recovery train (acid/alkali leach, magnetic/concentrate steps for Fe, SX/EW for Cu/Ni/Zn, cementation for Pb; REE-specific chemistries) conditioned by mineralogy and drilling fluid chemistry. <cite id="602407f5-0">Leach → separation (SX/ion exchange/adsorption) → EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Rapid Pb/Zn extraction at high alkalinity; oxidants/microwaves accelerate kinetics</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">pH-selective SX for Cu/Ni/Zn</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogy dictates REE leaching pathway and drilling fluid impacts surface chemistry</cite>.  
- Node C: Downcycling to construction/infrastructure (graded aggregates, road base, cement/plaster, asphalts) and environmental functions (adsorbents/catalysts, backfill), coupled with reuse of recovered oil in drilling fluids to close-loop. <cite id="62147b4a-0">De-oiled cuttings qualify for road paving and cement/plaster production</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Civil construction reuse and pollutant removal applications for decontaminated cuttings</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing drilling cost</cite>.

Routing decision framework (how to choose)
- If oil content >5% and clean water-based cuttings: centrifuge/leach to produce <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement; co-produce oil for energy or fuel; recycle solvents; optional hydromet for entrained fines. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to 1:3 ratio, >60 °C/30 min, achieves <1% oil cuttings for paving/cement with recyclable solvent and oil</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquid process enables integrated separation and solvent recovery</cite>.  
- If oil-based cuttings or mixed hydrocarbons: prefer solvent leaching or supercritical CO2 to extract 40–50% oil; for heavier decontamination, microwave/pyrolysis to <2% oil and >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min. <cite id="62147b4a-1">Leaching solvent achieves oil on cuttings <0.6% with recyclable streams</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">CO2 extraction up to 49% at 200 bar; microwave/thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% with >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite>.  
- If metal-rich formations or tool-wear fines present: hydromet flowsheet with condition optimization (acid/alkali type, temperature, oxidants, microwave) to maximize extraction and route Cu/Ni/Zn to SX/EW and Pb to cementation; REEs follow mineralogically matched chemistries with pre-leach contamination abatement. <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy effective for Cu with broader metal suite recoveries but with wastewater/residue handling needs</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching 80 °C (1–4 M NaOH) extracts Pb (~60%) and Zn (~58%) rapidly</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Drilling fluid effects and mineralogical host-phase specificity require tailored leaching</cite>.  
- If primarily rock fragments for geotechnical work: size-separate and clean polymer/bentonite coatings; stabilize and reuse as backfill/road base or convert to cement-bound stabilizers; entrained drilling fluid recovered for reuse. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Cleaning and sieving reduce cross-contamination and enable representative reuse</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings for construction and environmental applications</cite>.

5) Implementation trade-offs, risks, and enablers
- Composition uncertainty and contamination: drilling fluids’ mineral inputs and polymers cause size/morphology overlaps; rigorous cleaning and per-case correction are needed to avoid misclassification and downstream failures. <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling fluid granulation overlaps with mineral components; washing removes fines unpredictably; magnets remove casing fragments; per-case XRD correction is recommended</cite>.  
- Process intensity and costs: solvent leaching and pyrolysis show strong oil recovery but require energy and reagent management; supercritical CO2 offers high selectivity at significant pressure costs; hydromet flowsheets must manage acid/base hazards, residues, and wastewater. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching conditions and solvent/oil recycling reduce costs and environmental burden</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Microwave/thermal decontamination achieves deep oil removal and high recovery at elevated temperatures and times</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s long times, acid hazards, heavy metal contamination risks, residues, and wastewater are key limitations</cite>.  
- Regulatory and market readiness: reuse in civil construction and environmental applications is supported, but quality specifications for aggregates and adsorbents must be met; oil recovery quality dictates whether it closes-loop into drilling muds or downcycles. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Valorization into construction and environmental sectors is documented with case studies and legal aspects, encouraging sustainable strategies</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing drilling cost</cite>.  
- Mineralogy-driven personalization: adopting a mineral-first decision tree prevents one-size-fits-all failures; REE-bearing cuttings from carbonates/shales require tailored leaching chemistries and drilling-fluid-aware protocols. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided extraction with decision-tree alignment improves recoverability and sustainability</cite>.

Practical blueprint across drilling operations
1) At the wellsite or MUD/processing facility, implement a cleaning hub (magnets, cyclones, high-pressure wash, dedicated sieves) with pXRF/XRD on split samples; correct for fines loss and drilling-fluid overlap. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Sampling/cleaning steps reduce cross-contamination</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Cleaning and per-case correction recommended</cite>.  
2) Route to oil recovery train based on fluid type: solvent leaching or supercritical CO2 for oil-based systems; microwave/pyrolysis for mixed/old cuttings; target <1–0.6% residual oil before solids reuse. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to <1% oil enables aggregates/cement reuse with solvent/oil recycling</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">CO2 extraction up to 49% at 200 bar; thermal routes to <1.87% oil with >98% recovery</cite>.  
3) De-oiled solids enter a hydromet screening: acid/alkali leach for entrained fines and matrix-hosted metals; separate Cu/Ni/Zn via SX/EW and Pb via cementation (or electrorefining), with REEs following host-phase-specific protocols. <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydromet flowsheet: leach → SX/ion exchange/adsorption → EW/cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Rapid alkaline extraction of Pb/Zn with kinetics improved by oxidants/microwaves</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE extraction matched to host phases with drilling-fluid-aware leaching</cite>.  
4) Tailings and fines go to circular construction: stabilized road base, cement/plaster raw meal, or engineered fills; polymer/bentonite fines can be adsorbents/catalysts if certified. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Civil construction reuse and pollutant removal applications for decontaminated cuttings</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">De-oiled cuttings used as cement/plaster raw materials and road pavers</cite>.  
5) Close loops: return extracted oil to drilling muds and recovered drilling solids to mud conditioning; track TEA and LCA continuously to adapt intensity and chemistry per operation. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing cost</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Integrated ionic liquid recovery supports closed-loop material reuse</cite>.

Evidence gaps and how to close them
Direct techno-economic comparisons across offshore/onshore/geothermal operations and long-term performance of decontaminated cuttings in pavements/backfill are thin in the retrieved snippets; however, the quantitative oil recovery windows and hydromet kinetics, combined with mineralogy-driven decision frameworks, provide actionable conditions to pilot multi-node valorization. Prioritize pilots that quantify: (a) oil yield vs energy/capex; (b) metal extraction grade/recovery vs lixiviant and pretreatment; and (c) long-term performance of aggregate/cement products. Use site-specific pXRF/XRD and drilling-fluid composition to tune leach pH/temperature and select SX chemistries. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Decision-tree alignment to mineralogy improves recovery and sustainability</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s selectivity and constraints guide chemistry choice and downstream integration</cite>.

Bottom line
There is no universal “best” pathway; the valorization route that maximizes resource recovery across drilling operations is a modular, integrated superstructure: decontaminate first (washing, magnetic/cyclonic separation, and analytics), then branch by contaminant and mineralogy—extract oil and drilling fluid to <1% residual for reuse or energy, recover metals via hydromet flowsheets tuned to host phases, and convert de-oiled solids to construction/industrial feeds—closing loops with solvent/oil reuse and regulatory-compliant product markets. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Decontamination to <1% oil unlocks road/cement reuse with solvent/oil recycling</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 and thermal routes provide 40–50% oil extraction and >98% recovery under optimized conditions</cite> <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydrometallurgical flowsheets recover multiple metals from leach liquors via SX/EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided extraction strategies turn cuttings from waste to strategic critical-mineral sources</cite>.

Title: A Mineralogical Perspective on Rare Earth Elements (REEs) Extraction from Drill Cuttings: A Review
Snippet: The growing demand for rare earth elements (REEs) in high-tech and green energy sectors has prompted renewed exploration of unconventional sources. Drill cuttings, which are commonly discarded during subsurface drilling, are increasingly recognized as a potentially valuable, underutilized secondary REE reservoir. This review adopts a mineral-first lens to assess REE occurrence, extractability, and recovery strategies from drill cuttings across various lithologies. Emphasis is placed on how REEs associate with specific mineral host phases ranging from ion-adsorbed clays and organically bound forms to structurally integrated phosphates, each dictating distinct leaching pathways. The impact of drilling fluids on REE surface chemistry and mineral integrity is critically examined, alongside an evaluation of analytical and extraction methods tailored to different host phases. A scenario-based qualitative techno-economic assessment and a novel decision-tree framework are introduced to align mineralogy with optimal recovery strategies. Limitations in prior studies, particularly in characterization workflows and mineralogical misalignment in leaching protocols, are highlighted. This review redefines drill cuttings from industrial waste to a strategic resource, advocating for mineralogically guided extraction approaches to enhance sustainability in the critical mineral supply chain.
</snippet>

Snippet: The decontaminated drill cutting can be used in civil construction or can be repurposed in the environmental sector as adsorbents or catalysts for removing pollutants from wastewater (Yang et al. 2022a). Additionally, there is an opportunity to implement global-scale treatment and valorization solutions for drill cuttings contaminated (de Almeida et al. 2017;Cherepovitsyn and Lebedev 2023). 

Although prior studies have addressed specific aspects of drilling waste management, there is a notable scarcity of integrated reviews that link the technical complexities of drilling with the quantitative characterization and valorization of drill cuttings. This article aims to address this knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive view, from waste generation to potential reuse. This review is organized into the following topics: (1) Types of oil well drilling; (2) Drilling fluids; (3) Toxicity of drilling fluids; (4) Characterization methods of drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids; (5) Risk assessment; (6) Treatment technologies for drill cuttings management; (7) Valorization of drill cuttings; (8) Case studies and pilot-scale trials (9) Innovative advances in treatment; and (9) Legal aspects. This work is of particular importance in stimulating discussion and providing a foundational reference for those developing or implementing strategies for drill cutting management, thereby supporting more sustainable practices in the oil industry.
</snippet>

Snippet: The coring and collection of rock cuttings included the following two procedures: (1) Coring. In the HDD borehole, intermittent coring was carried out using a diamond coring drill, as shown in Figure 7. The core position in the borehole can be set in the mutation section, softer lithologic section, and critical point of the fault zone of tunnel construction. Before coring, the target interval was selected based on the designed depth, trajectory record, and drilling response. After retrieval, core length, recovery rate, RQD, photographs, and lithological descriptions were recorded on site. The procedure for HDD coring involves several steps. When the tri-cone drill bit reaches the designed position, the DTA is fully withdrawn. The diamond coring drill and single-action-double-pipe drilling tool are then installed and pushed to the coring position for the coring operation. After coring, all the drilling tools are pulled out. This operation is repeated until all the coring work is completed. 

(2) Collection of rock cuttings. As shown in Figure 8a,b, during drilling, a 100-mesh sieve with an aperture size of 0.15 mm was used at the borehole collar to collect the returning cuttings. The cuttings were collected at a fixed drilling advance interval of 10 m, and each sample was bagged immediately after collection. This fixed-interval sampling strategy was adopted to ensure the continuity and representativeness of the cutting samples along the borehole. The depth and sample ID were recorded on each bag (Figure 8c). Each cutting sample was assigned a unique ID, and the corresponding depth, sampling time, and drill-pipe number were recorded. The sieve was cleaned before sampling to reduce cross-contamination. The recorded collection depth was later corrected using the calculated cutting-lag distance. After completion of the cutting collection, the samples were subjected to XRD analysis and macroscopic characterization. Before XRD analysis, visible drillingmud coatings and soft residues on the cuttings were removed as far as possible to reduce the potential influence of bentonite and polymer additives. Finally, a vibrating sieve was used to determine the particle-size distribution of the cuttings (Figure 8d).

Because of the necessity to reduce costs, coring is most frequently conducted on a fragmentary basis, and in the remaining part of the borehole, less expensive drill cuttings are collected. The reconstruction of a lithological profile for the entire borehole interval requires combining results gained for both types of research material. 

There is one more problem concerning the procedure of cuttings cleaning before milling. Cuttings are usually contaminated with components of drilling fluid, which is a mixture of fluids and solids. The most basic function of a drilling fluid is the transportation of drilled cuttings to the surface. Reaching the surface, cuttings are mechanically removed from the fluid before it is recirculated downhole, but they are never completely devoid of solid drilling fluid components. The problem arises because drilling fluid components are usually minerals (for example bentonite clay, barite, calcium carbonate or hematite) and their granulation overlaps with granulation of cuttings mineral components. Sometimes, cuttings are also contaminated by fragments of damaged borehole casing, which is easy to remove with the use of neodymium magnet. 

As mentioned above, cuttings are usually extremely inhomogeneous and contain grains of different sizes. The granulation of cuttings is usually dependent on the technic of drilling (the applied drill bit), lithology, mineralogy, and geomechanical properties of drilled rocks. Every washing of cutting leads to the uncontrolled removal of the finest grain fractions, usually clay minerals and the softest minerals. It changes the mineralogy of cuttings in ways that are hard to predict, unless we can get clean rock chips. In our opinion, the better solution is to make the proper result correction after XRD analysis. This should be carefully examined for each individual case. Our results show that, in some cases, there is no need to make correction at all. 

Conducting measurements on drill cuttings implies the necessity of carrying out measurements on milled material.

Title: Study on the effect of innovative leaching solvent on the oil removal for oily drilling cuttings
Snippet: A new type of leaching solvent for oily drilling cuttings was developed, and the effect of leaching solvent on the oil removal for oily cuttings was investigated. The results indicated that the leaching solvent had good capacity of oil removal for oily cuttings, and the oil content of treated cuttings is less than 0.6%. The leaching solvent could be separated from the oil phase through distillation, and the recyclable solvent could be reused to treat other cuttings. Moreover, oil resources adsorbed on the oily cuttings could be recycled and reused to prepare new drilling fluids, so the drilling cost could be reduced greatly. As a result, the leaching solvent could treat the oily cuttings effectively, and recycle and reuse oil resources, and thus produce great economic benefits. It can play an essential role in safe drilling jobs and improvement of drilling efficiency in the future.

Snippet: Extraction with supercritical fluids is a thermochemical separation process in which H 2 O and CO 2 are subjected to pressures and temperatures that cause their dielectric constants to decrease, and the solubility of both becomes similar to that of organic solvents (Radfarnia et al. 2015;Hu et al. 2022). When used for the extraction of oily fluids from drill cuttings, it was possible to extract up to 49% of the oily fluid from the drill cuttings using a pressure of 200 bar and a flow rate of 56.02 cm 3 /s of CO 2 (Goodarznia and Esmaeilzadeh 2006). However, this process is still little reported for the Fig. 5 Treatment options and potential reuse for drill cuttings treatment of drill cuttings, being more commonly used in the treatment of oily sludge (Pereira et al. 2022). 

When it comes to thermal processes, the most used ways for separating drill cuttings from fluids by using temperature are pyrolysis and microwave heating. Pyrolysis occurs through endo and exothermic processes, with stages of heating, vaporization, and cracking of the hydrocarbons adhered to the drill cuttings (Xu et al. 2023;Wang et al. 2024d). After the molecules broken, they are desorbed, reducing the oil content present in the drill cuttings. At the end, the small desorbed molecular fragments can be rearranged and resynthesized into petroleum hydrocarbons for the recovery and reuse of the oily fluid (Xu et al. 2023). This decontamination process is widely studied since it does not generate secondary pollutants, and the products (solids, liquids, and gases) can be recovered for reuse (Hou et al. 2018). Liu et al. (2023a), when evaluating the pyrolysis process in drill cuttings, achieved a reduction from 8.03% to 1.87% of oily fluid in the drill cuttings. They also observed that a recovery rate of over 98% of the oil could be obtained in residence times greater than 50 min and at temperatures above 350 °C.

Snippet: Chalcopyrites, pentaldite, spent catalyst, batteries, brass ash, zinc ash are some of the major sources for the production of copper, nickel and zinc 1 . Apart from sulfides, significant resources for these metals are available as oxide/silicate deposits. These raw materials are subjected to various hydrometallurgical treatments which include atmospheric/pressure/bioleaching of sulfate/chloride solutions. The leach liquor, thus obtained contains copper, nickel, zinc along with some impurities such as iron, chromium, aluminium, silicon etc. Liquid-liquid extraction has been applied to many solutions to obtain either metals or their salts in highly pure form, as these metals are industrially and economically more important and therefore there is a great need to separate and recover them. Solvent extraction has been carried out extensively for the separation of cobalt and nickel with alkyl phosphorus reagents like Cyanex 272 and D2EHPA 2,3 . Similarly Chelating reagents like LIX 87QN, LIX 54, LIX 973, LIX 34, LIX 984, LIX 984N and LIX 84I have been used for the extraction, separation and recovery of copper, nickel and zinc from ammonium carbonate / ammonium sulfate solutions [4][5][6][7][8][9][10] . Extraction of copper, nickel and zinc from their sulfate solutions, using LIX 84I was found to depend on the equilibrium pH of the aqueous phase 11,12 . It was found that LIX 984N was very selective for copper extraction. In this paper, we report the solvent extraction separation of copper, nickel and zinc from synthetic solution using LIX 984 N as the extractant dissolved in kerosene, with an aim to separate these metals efficiently by single stage extraction. On the basis of this, a flow sheet of the process has been developed.

Summary
Maximizing resource recovery from drill cuttings and rock fragments requires a context-adaptive, multi-node valorization “superstructure” that first cleans and characterizes the material, then departs into parallel tracks: oil/wax and drilling-fluid solids recovery; hydrometallurgical or physical recovery of base/precious metals and critical elements; and downcycling into construction/industrial feeds (e.g., cement raw meal, graded aggregates). This approach aligns mineralogy, contamination state, and market viability to maximize total value; process windows with demonstrated performance include solvent/thermal decontamination to <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement, supercritical CO2 extraction up to ~49% oil, and hydromet flowsheets (leach → SX/EW or cementation) for Cu/Ni/Zn depending on host phases and drilling fluid chemistry. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Drill cuttings are a heterogeneous, underutilized secondary reservoir for critical elements, and recovery must be mineralogy-guided due to variable REE host phases and drilling-fluid effects</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can be reused in civil construction or deployed as adsorbents/catalysts; integrated reviews emphasize full chains from generation to reuse with case studies and legal aspects</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-2">Rigorous sampling, cleaning, and size separation are needed to avoid cross-contamination and bias in composition</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-3">Offshore cuttings comprise mixed lithologies from sands to limestones; their fine, disaggregated nature complicates analysis and use</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling-mud components (bentonite, barite, carbonates) overlap with mineral grains and must be accounted for; cleaning and per-case correction are recommended</cite>.

1) Why a single, fixed “pathway” fails
Drill cuttings are inherently heterogeneous mixtures of rock fragments, entrained drilling fluid solids, and adsorbed hydrocarbons, with compositions that shift by lithology (carbonates, shales, sandstones), drilling fluid type (water-based vs oil-based), and operational regime (offshore HDD, geothermal, mining). <cite id="3d07b152-3">Offshore sequences produce mixed lithologies (sandstone, siltstone, shale, limestone) in silt-to-fine-sand fractions</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/calcite hematite inputs and casing fragments complicate mineralogy and require cleaning to avoid misattribution</cite>. Their metal content arises from both matrix minerals and drilling-fluid cuttings (e.g., bentonite clays), so recovery strategies must separate entrained solids and account for contamination before any extraction. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Cleaning and sieving protocols reduce cross-contamination and enable representative sampling</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling fluid granulations overlap with mineral grains; improper washing alters mineralogy and composition unpredictably</cite>. A single pathway cannot globally “maximize” recovery; instead, a modular decision framework should route cuttings through pre-treatment, analytics, and parallel recovery trains tuned to host mineralogy and contamination. <cite id="3d07b152-0">A mineral-first framework links REE host phases to distinct leaching pathways and proposes a decision-tree to align mineralogy with extraction methods</cite>.

2) Core unit operations and interfaces
- Characterization and decontamination. Sieving, washing, and mechanical removal of drilling fluid solids (e.g., bentonite, barite) and casing fragments are prerequisites; magnets can remove ferrous fragments, while density/centrifugal separation can target barite and clays. <cite id="3d07b152-2">A 100-mesh sieve and fixed-interval sampling cleaned of mud coatings reduce cross-contamination</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/carbonates are common drilling-fluid inputs overlapping in size; casing fragments can be magnetically removed</cite>. Analytics (pXRF, XRD, SEM/MLA) guide downstream choices and correct for comminution/cleaning effects. <cite id="3d07b152-3">SEM-automated mineralogy reveals mixed lithologies in fine grains</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">pXRF on cuttings requires comminution and correction for cleaning-induced loss of fines</cite>.
- Oil and drilling-fluid oil recovery. Centrifugation, leaching with selective solvents, and thermal routes separate oil and entrained drilling fluid; de-oiled cuttings then qualify for construction reuse. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching with optimized solvent/temperature/time (e.g., 1:3 cutting:solvent ratio, >60 °C for 30 min) efficiently removes oil from oily cuttings to <1% residual, enabling road paving or cement/plaster feed; recyclable solvent and oil can be looped back for reuse</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-1">A novel leaching solvent achieved oil on cuttings below 0.6% with recyclable solvent/oil streams, reducing costs and enabling reuse</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 can extract up to 49% oily fluid at 200 bar; microwave/thermal decontamination reduces oil from 8.03% to 1.87% and can achieve >98% oil recovery at >350 °C and >50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids enable effective separation of drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery for reuse, supporting integrated management to enhance material recovery</cite>.
- Metals and critical elements recovery. Hydrometallurgical flowsheets (acid/alkali leach → separation via solvent extraction, ion exchange, adsorption → electrowinning/cementation) recover Cu, Ni, Zn, Pb, and others depending on host and lixiviants; process intensity (temperature, time, oxidants, microwave) tunes extraction kinetics. <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydrometallurgy uses acid/caustic leaching followed by separation (SX, ion exchange, adsorption) and metal recovery via electrorefining/EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy is effective for Cu and can extract Fe, Sn, Zn, Al, Ni, Pb depending on lixiviant and downstream strategy; challenges include long times, acid hazards, heavy metal contamination risks, residues, and wastewater</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching (1–4 M NaOH, 20–80 °C) can extract Pb ~60% in 15 min at 80 °C and Zn ~58% at 4 M NaOH; intensification via oxidants or microwaves increases leaching efficiency</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">Solvent extraction with LIX 984N selectively extracts Cu from sulfate solutions; extraction depends on pH and enables separation of Cu/Ni/Zn</cite> <cite id="602407f5-4">Leaching, SX, and EW are core steps for oxide ores; cementation is a cheaper, less selective alternative to recover copper from pregnant solutions</cite>. Mineralogy-guided leaching is key: organically bound or ion-adsorbed REEs require different chemistries than structurally integrated phosphates, and drilling fluids alter surface chemistry and integrity. <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE occurrence across host phases (ion-adsorbed clays, organically bound, structurally integrated phosphates) dictates distinct leaching pathways; drilling fluids influence surface chemistry and integrity, requiring matched extraction methods</cite>.
- Downcycling to construction/industrial feeds. De-oiled, de-sanded cuttings can be stabilized and used for road base or as raw materials in cement and plaster; pre-treatment to <1% oil and removal of ferrous/casing fragments improves compliance and performance. <cite id="62147b4a-0">After leaching to <1% oil, cuttings can be paved or used as cement/plaster raw materials; recyclable oil and solvent reduce costs and pollution</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated drill cuttings can be reused in civil construction and repurposed as adsorbents/catalysts for wastewater treatment</cite>. For rock fragments from geotechnical drilling (HDD or tunneling), sieving and cleaning enable graded sands/fines for construction or environmental media. <cite id="3d07b152-2">A 100-mesh sieve and careful cleaning of bentonite/polymer residues yield representative, cross-contaminant-reduced cuttings for reuse</cite>.

3) Operation-specific valorization pathways
Offshore oil and gas (rig-based, marine)  
- Pre-treatment and analytics: high-pressure washing, magnetic removal, and density-based barite/bentonite separation; pXRF/XRD to classify lithologies and contamination. <cite id="3d07b152-4">Bentonite/barite/carbonates overlap in size with minerals; cleaning/correction is required to avoid misattribution</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-3">Mixed lithologies and comminuted fines complicate use; SEM-MLA informs provenance and mineralogy</cite>.  
- Oil/wax and drilling-fluid recovery: combine solvent leaching and/or microwave/thermal decontamination to produce oil-free cuttings for aggregates/cement while closing-looping oil and drilling fluid. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to 1:3 ratio, >60 °C/30 min, yields <1% oil cuttings for paving/cement; solvent and oil are recyclable</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 extracts up to 49% at 200 bar; microwave/thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% and enable >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids separate drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery, enabling integrated reuse</cite>.  
- Metals recovery: where cuttings contain sulfides/oxides or drilling-derived metal fines (e.g., steel tool fragments), hydromet flowsheets recover ferrous/non-ferrous metals; selective SX/EW for Cu/Ni/Zn and cementation for Pb. <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy effectively recovers Cu and can target Fe, Sn, Zn, Ni, Pb depending on lixiviants and separation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching at 80 °C (1–4 M NaOH) extracts Pb (~60%) and Zn (~58%) rapidly; oxidants/microwaves accelerate kinetics</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">LIX 984N selectively extracts Cu; pH controls selectivity for Cu/Ni/Zn separation</cite>.  
- Side-streams to circular markets: decontaminated fines as adsorbents/catalysts and construction fill; oil recovered can be reprocessed as make-up for drilling fluids. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can serve as adsorbents/catalysts for pollutant removal and as construction fill</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing costs</cite>.

Onshore oil and gas/geothermal/mineral drilling  
- Pre-treatment adapted to formation lithology: carbonate-rich zones benefit from acid leaching to desorb drilling fluid and mobilize fines; clay-rich zones need gentle pH-tuned leaching to avoid dispersion. <cite id="602407f5-2">Leaching conditions (concentration, temperature, time) and porosity control diffusion and efficiency; alkaline leaching efficiently removes Pb/Zn from oxide-like dusts</cite>.  
- Metals focus: where formations host oxide/hydroxide or sulfide minerals (e.g., Cu-bearing carbonates, Ni/Co laterites), hydromet flowsheets recover multiple metals with SX/EW or cementation; REEs in drilling mud-bearing shales require acid/carbonate systems matched to host phases. <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE occurrence governs leaching chemistry; drilling fluids alter surfaces, so extraction must align with host phase and contamination</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">Solvent extraction selectively separates Cu/Ni/Zn from sulfate solutions; pH control is central</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s selectivity and lower energy can extract a broader suite of metals but generates residues and wastewater needing treatment</cite>.  
- Oil and brine valorization: in geothermal brine environments, thermal/membrane separations can decontaminate cuttings and recover heat/beneficiaries; oil recovered supports energy recovery. <cite id="62147b4a-3">Pyrolysis/microwave heating desorb hydrocarbons with product streams recoverable for reuse; solids can proceed to aggregates/cement</cite>.  
- Aggregates and road base: de-oiled cuttings meeting <1% oil pass into stabilization or cement-bound mixes after ensuring absence of drilling fluid fines; careful cleaning prevents long-term performance degradation. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to <1% oil enables road paving or cement/plaster use; solvent/oil recycling improves sustainability</cite>.

High-density directional drilling (HDD) and tunneling  
- Episode-based valorization: collect cuttings with sieves/cyclones; clean polymer/bentonite coatings; size-grade for immediate reuse in backfill or environmental applications, then route de-oiled fractions into cement-bound materials. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Use of 100-mesh sieve and cleaning protocols yields representative, cross-contaminant-reduced cuttings</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings can be used for construction and environmental applications</cite>.  
- Metals and REEs in cored fragments: where cores include carbonatite/alkaline complexes, apply mineralogy-driven REE leaching; tool steel fragments are ferrosed by hydromet or magnetically recovered. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided REE extraction across host phases with decision-tree routing</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy recovers multiple metals with established flowsheets</cite>.

4) An integrated, multi-node “superstructure” to maximize total recovery
A robust valorization “superstructure” decouples contaminant removal from element-specific recovery, feeding multiple markets:
- Node A: Decontamination hub (centrifugation, leaching, ionic liquid/supercritical options) to produce oil-free, solids-depleted cuttings for construction reuse, while capturing oil, brine, and entrained drilling solids. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Solvent leaching achieves <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement with solvent and oil recyclability</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 extracts up to 49% oil at 200 bar; thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% with >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquids separate drilling fluid from cuttings with solvent recovery</cite>.  
- Node B: Hydrometallurgical recovery train (acid/alkali leach, magnetic/concentrate steps for Fe, SX/EW for Cu/Ni/Zn, cementation for Pb; REE-specific chemistries) conditioned by mineralogy and drilling fluid chemistry. <cite id="602407f5-0">Leach → separation (SX/ion exchange/adsorption) → EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Rapid Pb/Zn extraction at high alkalinity; oxidants/microwaves accelerate kinetics</cite> <cite id="602407f5-3">pH-selective SX for Cu/Ni/Zn</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogy dictates REE leaching pathway and drilling fluid impacts surface chemistry</cite>.  
- Node C: Downcycling to construction/infrastructure (graded aggregates, road base, cement/plaster, asphalts) and environmental functions (adsorbents/catalysts, backfill), coupled with reuse of recovered oil in drilling fluids to close-loop. <cite id="62147b4a-0">De-oiled cuttings qualify for road paving and cement/plaster production</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Civil construction reuse and pollutant removal applications for decontaminated cuttings</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing drilling cost</cite>.

Routing decision framework (how to choose)
- If oil content >5% and clean water-based cuttings: centrifuge/leach to produce <1% oil cuttings for aggregates/cement; co-produce oil for energy or fuel; recycle solvents; optional hydromet for entrained fines. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to 1:3 ratio, >60 °C/30 min, achieves <1% oil cuttings for paving/cement with recyclable solvent and oil</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Ionic liquid process enables integrated separation and solvent recovery</cite>.  
- If oil-based cuttings or mixed hydrocarbons: prefer solvent leaching or supercritical CO2 to extract 40–50% oil; for heavier decontamination, microwave/pyrolysis to <2% oil and >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min. <cite id="62147b4a-1">Leaching solvent achieves oil on cuttings <0.6% with recyclable streams</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">CO2 extraction up to 49% at 200 bar; microwave/thermal routes reduce oil to ~1.87% with >98% recovery at 350 °C/50 min</cite>.  
- If metal-rich formations or tool-wear fines present: hydromet flowsheet with condition optimization (acid/alkali type, temperature, oxidants, microwave) to maximize extraction and route Cu/Ni/Zn to SX/EW and Pb to cementation; REEs follow mineralogically matched chemistries with pre-leach contamination abatement. <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy effective for Cu with broader metal suite recoveries but with wastewater/residue handling needs</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Alkaline leaching 80 °C (1–4 M NaOH) extracts Pb (~60%) and Zn (~58%) rapidly</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Drilling fluid effects and mineralogical host-phase specificity require tailored leaching</cite>.  
- If primarily rock fragments for geotechnical work: size-separate and clean polymer/bentonite coatings; stabilize and reuse as backfill/road base or convert to cement-bound stabilizers; entrained drilling fluid recovered for reuse. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Cleaning and sieving reduce cross-contamination and enable representative reuse</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-1">Decontaminated cuttings for construction and environmental applications</cite>.

5) Implementation trade-offs, risks, and enablers
- Composition uncertainty and contamination: drilling fluids’ mineral inputs and polymers cause size/morphology overlaps; rigorous cleaning and per-case correction are needed to avoid misclassification and downstream failures. <cite id="3d07b152-4">Drilling fluid granulation overlaps with mineral components; washing removes fines unpredictably; magnets remove casing fragments; per-case XRD correction is recommended</cite>.  
- Process intensity and costs: solvent leaching and pyrolysis show strong oil recovery but require energy and reagent management; supercritical CO2 offers high selectivity at significant pressure costs; hydromet flowsheets must manage acid/base hazards, residues, and wastewater. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching conditions and solvent/oil recycling reduce costs and environmental burden</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Microwave/thermal decontamination achieves deep oil removal and high recovery at elevated temperatures and times</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s long times, acid hazards, heavy metal contamination risks, residues, and wastewater are key limitations</cite>.  
- Regulatory and market readiness: reuse in civil construction and environmental applications is supported, but quality specifications for aggregates and adsorbents must be met; oil recovery quality dictates whether it closes-loop into drilling muds or downcycles. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Valorization into construction and environmental sectors is documented with case studies and legal aspects, encouraging sustainable strategies</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids can be reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing drilling cost</cite>.  
- Mineralogy-driven personalization: adopting a mineral-first decision tree prevents one-size-fits-all failures; REE-bearing cuttings from carbonates/shales require tailored leaching chemistries and drilling-fluid-aware protocols. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided extraction with decision-tree alignment improves recoverability and sustainability</cite>.

Practical blueprint across drilling operations
1) At the wellsite or MUD/processing facility, implement a cleaning hub (magnets, cyclones, high-pressure wash, dedicated sieves) with pXRF/XRD on split samples; correct for fines loss and drilling-fluid overlap. <cite id="3d07b152-2">Sampling/cleaning steps reduce cross-contamination</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-4">Cleaning and per-case correction recommended</cite>.  
2) Route to oil recovery train based on fluid type: solvent leaching or supercritical CO2 for oil-based systems; microwave/pyrolysis for mixed/old cuttings; target <1–0.6% residual oil before solids reuse. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Leaching to <1% oil enables aggregates/cement reuse with solvent/oil recycling</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">CO2 extraction up to 49% at 200 bar; thermal routes to <1.87% oil with >98% recovery</cite>.  
3) De-oiled solids enter a hydromet screening: acid/alkali leach for entrained fines and matrix-hosted metals; separate Cu/Ni/Zn via SX/EW and Pb via cementation (or electrorefining), with REEs following host-phase-specific protocols. <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydromet flowsheet: leach → SX/ion exchange/adsorption → EW/cementation</cite> <cite id="602407f5-2">Rapid alkaline extraction of Pb/Zn with kinetics improved by oxidants/microwaves</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">REE extraction matched to host phases with drilling-fluid-aware leaching</cite>.  
4) Tailings and fines go to circular construction: stabilized road base, cement/plaster raw meal, or engineered fills; polymer/bentonite fines can be adsorbents/catalysts if certified. <cite id="3d07b152-1">Civil construction reuse and pollutant removal applications for decontaminated cuttings</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-0">De-oiled cuttings used as cement/plaster raw materials and road pavers</cite>.  
5) Close loops: return extracted oil to drilling muds and recovered drilling solids to mud conditioning; track TEA and LCA continuously to adapt intensity and chemistry per operation. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Recovered oil-based drilling fluids reused to prepare new drilling fluids, reducing cost</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-4">Integrated ionic liquid recovery supports closed-loop material reuse</cite>.

Evidence gaps and how to close them
Direct techno-economic comparisons across offshore/onshore/geothermal operations and long-term performance of decontaminated cuttings in pavements/backfill are thin in the retrieved snippets; however, the quantitative oil recovery windows and hydromet kinetics, combined with mineralogy-driven decision frameworks, provide actionable conditions to pilot multi-node valorization. Prioritize pilots that quantify: (a) oil yield vs energy/capex; (b) metal extraction grade/recovery vs lixiviant and pretreatment; and (c) long-term performance of aggregate/cement products. Use site-specific pXRF/XRD and drilling-fluid composition to tune leach pH/temperature and select SX chemistries. <cite id="3d07b152-0">Decision-tree alignment to mineralogy improves recovery and sustainability</cite> <cite id="602407f5-1">Hydrometallurgy’s selectivity and constraints guide chemistry choice and downstream integration</cite>.

Bottom line
There is no universal “best” pathway; the valorization route that maximizes resource recovery across drilling operations is a modular, integrated superstructure: decontaminate first (washing, magnetic/cyclonic separation, and analytics), then branch by contaminant and mineralogy—extract oil and drilling fluid to <1% residual for reuse or energy, recover metals via hydromet flowsheets tuned to host phases, and convert de-oiled solids to construction/industrial feeds—closing loops with solvent/oil reuse and regulatory-compliant product markets. <cite id="62147b4a-0">Decontamination to <1% oil unlocks road/cement reuse with solvent/oil recycling</cite> <cite id="62147b4a-3">Supercritical CO2 and thermal routes provide 40–50% oil extraction and >98% recovery under optimized conditions</cite> <cite id="602407f5-0">Hydrometallurgical flowsheets recover multiple metals from leach liquors via SX/EW or cementation</cite> <cite id="3d07b152-0">Mineralogically guided extraction strategies turn cuttings from waste to strategic critical-mineral sources</cite>.
