Title: A Mineralogical Perspective on Rare Earth Elements (REEs) Extraction from Drill Cuttings: A Review
Snippet: The growing demand for rare earth elements (REEs) in high-tech and green energy sectors has prompted renewed exploration of unconventional sources. Drill cuttings, which are commonly discarded during subsurface drilling, are increasingly recognized as a potentially valuable, underutilized secondary REE reservoir. This review adopts a mineral-first lens to assess REE occurrence, extractability, and recovery strategies from drill cuttings across various lithologies. Emphasis is placed on how REEs associate with specific mineral host phases ranging from ion-adsorbed clays and organically bound forms to structurally integrated phosphates, each dictating distinct leaching pathways. The impact of drilling fluids on REE surface chemistry and mineral integrity is critically examined, alongside an evaluation of analytical and extraction methods tailored to different host phases. A scenario-based qualitative techno-economic assessment and a novel decision-tree framework are introduced to align mineralogy with optimal recovery strategies. Limitations in prior studies, particularly in characterization workflows and mineralogical misalignment in leaching protocols, are highlighted. This review redefines drill cuttings from industrial waste to a strategic resource, advocating for mineralogically guided extraction approaches to enhance sustainability in the critical mineral supply chain.

Title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
Snippet: The decontaminated drill cutting can be used in civil construction or can be repurposed in the environmental sector as adsorbents or catalysts for removing pollutants from wastewater (Yang et al. 2022a). Additionally, there is an opportunity to implement global-scale treatment and valorization solutions for drill cuttings contaminated (de Almeida et al. 2017;Cherepovitsyn and Lebedev 2023). 

Although prior studies have addressed specific aspects of drilling waste management, there is a notable scarcity of integrated reviews that link the technical complexities of drilling with the quantitative characterization and valorization of drill cuttings. This article aims to address this knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive view, from waste generation to potential reuse. This review is organized into the following topics: (1) Types of oil well drilling; (2) Drilling fluids; (3) Toxicity of drilling fluids; (4) Characterization methods of drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids; (5) Risk assessment; (6) Treatment technologies for drill cuttings management; (7) Valorization of drill cuttings; (8) Case studies and pilot-scale trials (9) Innovative advances in treatment; and (9) Legal aspects. This work is of particular importance in stimulating discussion and providing a foundational reference for those developing or implementing strategies for drill cutting management, thereby supporting more sustainable practices in the oil industry.

Title: The Application of Horizontal Directional Drilling for the Geological Investigation of Super-Long Tunnels: A Case Study
Snippet: The coring and collection of rock cuttings included the following two procedures: (1) Coring. In the HDD borehole, intermittent coring was carried out using a diamond coring drill, as shown in Figure 7. The core position in the borehole can be set in the mutation section, softer lithologic section, and critical point of the fault zone of tunnel construction. Before coring, the target interval was selected based on the designed depth, trajectory record, and drilling response. After retrieval, core length, recovery rate, RQD, photographs, and lithological descriptions were recorded on site. The procedure for HDD coring involves several steps. When the tri-cone drill bit reaches the designed position, the DTA is fully withdrawn. The diamond coring drill and single-action-double-pipe drilling tool are then installed and pushed to the coring position for the coring operation. After coring, all the drilling tools are pulled out. This operation is repeated until all the coring work is completed. 

(2) Collection of rock cuttings. As shown in Figure 8a,b, during drilling, a 100-mesh sieve with an aperture size of 0.15 mm was used at the borehole collar to collect the returning cuttings. The cuttings were collected at a fixed drilling advance interval of 10 m, and each sample was bagged immediately after collection. This fixed-interval sampling strategy was adopted to ensure the continuity and representativeness of the cutting samples along the borehole. The depth and sample ID were recorded on each bag (Figure 8c). Each cutting sample was assigned a unique ID, and the corresponding depth, sampling time, and drill-pipe number were recorded. The sieve was cleaned before sampling to reduce cross-contamination. The recorded collection depth was later corrected using the calculated cutting-lag distance. After completion of the cutting collection, the samples were subjected to XRD analysis and macroscopic characterization. Before XRD analysis, visible drillingmud coatings and soft residues on the cuttings were removed as far as possible to reduce the potential influence of bentonite and polymer additives. Finally, a vibrating sieve was used to determine the particle-size distribution of the cuttings (Figure 8d).

Title: High-Throughput Analysis of Offshore Well Drill-Cuttings via SEM-Automated Mineralogy Using Single-Step Trans-Vertical Moulds
Snippet: The material examined in this study was drill (i.e., well) cuttings, which consist of broken rock fragments derived from the drilling of an offshore borehole. The boreholes from which the cuttings were derived had been drilled in the offshore Newfoundland Grand Banks. In contrast with solid drill core, due to their broken, fine-grained disaggregated natures, cuttings material is typically very difficult to use for petrographic and textural studies. Though originally designed for use on mine sites and mining applications, SEM-MLA can provide insight into depositional environments, provenance, and petroleum system potential when applied to sedimentary samples, as first summarised by Sylvester [10] and used by others [9,11,12]. 

The sample material represented a wide variety of lithologies ranging from sandstone through siltstones and shales to limestones. In many samples, fragments of all these lithologies are mixed together. The grain sizes of the cutting materials analysed in this study ranged from 75 to 180 µm, which is essentially silt to fine sand-sized. Lithic fragments of finer-grained material, such as shale, however, were also observed in the SEM-MLA analysis. As the cutting materials represent broken, crushed rock, medium to coarse sandsized particles, if present in the well interval, they would be represented in the samples as fragments of larger grains.

Title: Downhole Lithological Profile Reconstruction Based on Chemical Composition of Core Samples and Drill Cuttings Measured with Portable X-ray Fluorescence Spectrometer
Snippet: At the beginning, the analysis was conducted with regard to the impact of rock material comminution degree on results obtained with the use of a pXRF owing to the fact that, during hydrocarbon exploration, mineralogical investigation is carried out both on solid samples coming from full size and sidewall cores as well as on drill cuttings collected during borehole drilling when cores are not collected. Because of the necessity to reduce costs, coring is most frequently conducted on a fragmentary basis, and in the remaining part of the borehole, less expensive drill cuttings are collected. The reconstruction of a lithological profile for the entire borehole interval requires combining results gained for both types of research material. 

There is one more problem concerning the procedure of cuttings cleaning before milling. Cuttings are usually contaminated with components of drilling fluid, which is a mixture of fluids and solids. The most basic function of a drilling fluid is the transportation of drilled cuttings to the surface. Reaching the surface, cuttings are mechanically removed from the fluid before it is recirculated downhole, but they are never completely devoid of solid drilling fluid components. The problem arises because drilling fluid components are usually minerals (for example bentonite clay, barite, calcium carbonate or hematite) and their granulation overlaps with granulation of cuttings mineral components. Sometimes, cuttings are also contaminated by fragments of damaged borehole casing, which is easy to remove with the use of neodymium magnet. 

As mentioned above, cuttings are usually extremely inhomogeneous and contain grains of different sizes. The granulation of cuttings is usually dependent on the technic of drilling (the applied drill bit), lithology, mineralogy, and geomechanical properties of drilled rocks. Every washing of cutting leads to the uncontrolled removal of the finest grain fractions, usually clay minerals and the softest minerals. It changes the mineralogy of cuttings in ways that are hard to predict, unless we can get clean rock chips. In our opinion, the better solution is to make the proper result correction after XRD analysis. This should be carefully examined for each individual case. Our results show that, in some cases, there is no need to make correction at all. 

Conducting measurements on drill cuttings implies the necessity of carrying out measurements on milled material.

When the tri-cone drill bit reaches the designed position, the DTA is fully withdrawn. The diamond coring drill and single-action-double-pipe drilling tool are then installed and pushed to the coring position for the coring operation. After coring, all the drilling tools are pulled out. This operation is repeated until all the coring work is completed.

The cuttings were collected at a fixed drilling advance interval of 10 m, and each sample was bagged immediately after collection. snippet.text:
The material examined in this study was drill (i.e., well) cuttings, which consist of broken rock fragments derived from the drilling of an offshore borehole. The boreholes from which the cuttings were derived had been drilled in the offshore Newfoundland Grand Banks. In contrast with solid drill core, due to their broken, fine-grained disaggregated natures, cuttings material is typically very difficult to use for petrographic and textural studies. Though originally designed for use on mine sites and mining applications, SEM-MLA can provide insight into depositional environments, provenance, and petroleum system potential when applied to sedimentary samples, as first summarised by Sylvester [10] and used by others [9,11,12]. 

The sample material represented a wide variety of lithologies ranging from sandstone through siltstones and shales to limestones. In many samples, fragments of all these lithologies are mixed together. The grain sizes of the cutting materials analysed in this study ranged from 75 to 180 µm, which is essentially silt to fine sand-sized. Lithic fragments of finer-grained material, such as shale, however, were also observed in the SEM-MLA analysis. As the cutting materials represent broken, crushed rock, medium to coarse sandsized particles, if present in the well interval, they would be represented in the samples as fragments of larger grains.

snippet.text:
At the beginning, the analysis was conducted with regard to the impact of rock material comminution degree on results obtained with the use of a pXRF owing to the fact that, during hydrocarbon exploration, mineralogical investigation is carried out both on solid samples coming from full size and sidewall cores as well as on drill cuttings collected during borehole drilling when cores are not collected. Because of the necessity to reduce costs, coring is most frequently conducted on a fragmentary basis, and in the remaining part of the borehole, less expensive drill cuttings are collected. The reconstruction of a lithological profile for the entire borehole interval requires combining results gained for both types of research material. 

There is one more problem concerning the procedure of cuttings cleaning before milling. Cuttings are usually contaminated with components of drilling fluid, which is a mixture of fluids and solids. The most basic function of a drilling fluid is the transportation of drilled cuttings to the surface. Reaching the surface, cuttings are mechanically removed from the fluid before it is recirculated downhole, but they are never completely devoid of solid drilling fluid components. The problem arises because drilling fluid components are usually minerals (for example bentonite clay, barite, calcium carbonate or hematite) and their granulation overlaps with granulation of cuttings mineral components. Sometimes, cuttings are also contaminated by fragments of damaged borehole casing, which is easy to remove with the use of neodymium magnet. 

As mentioned above, cuttings are usually extremely inhomogeneous and contain grains of different sizes. The granulation of cuttings is usually dependent on the technic of drilling (the applied drill bit), lithology, mineralogy, and geomechanical properties of drilled rocks. Every washing of cutting leads to the uncontrolled removal of the finest grain fractions, usually clay minerals and the softest minerals. It changes the mineralogy of cuttings in ways that are hard to predict, unless we can get clean rock chips. In our opinion, the better solution is to make the proper result correction after XRD analysis. This should be carefully examined for each individual case. Our results show that, in some cases, there is no need to make correction at all. 

Conducting measurements on drill cuttings implies the necessity of carrying out measurements on milled material.

documents.title: A Mineralogical Perspective on Rare Earth Elements (REEs) Extraction from Drill Cuttings: A Review
documents.snippet: The growing demand for rare earth elements (REEs) in high-tech and green energy sectors has prompted renewed exploration of unconventional sources. Drill cuttings, which are commonly discarded during subsurface drilling, are increasingly recognized as a potentially valuable, underutilized secondary REE reservoir. This review adopts a mineral-first lens to assess REE occurrence, extractability, and recovery strategies from drill cuttings across various lithologies. Emphasis is placed on how REEs associate with specific mineral host phases ranging from ion-adsorbed clays and organically bound forms to structurally integrated phosphates, each dictating distinct leaching pathways. The impact of drilling fluids on REE surface chemistry and mineral integrity is critically examined, alongside an evaluation of analytical and extraction methods tailored to different host phases. A scenario-based qualitative techno-economic assessment and a novel decision-tree framework are introduced to align mineralogy with optimal recovery strategies. Limitations in prior studies, particularly in characterization workflows and mineralogical misalignment in leaching protocols, are highlighted. This review redefines drill cuttings from industrial waste to a strategic resource, advocating for mineralogically guided extraction approaches to enhance sustainability in the critical mineral supply chain.

documents.title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
documents.snippet:
The decontaminated drill cutting can be used in civil construction or can be repurposed in the environmental sector as adsorbents or catalysts for removing pollutants from wastewater (Yang et al. 2022a). Additionally, there is an opportunity to implement global-scale treatment and valorization solutions for drill cuttings contaminated (de Almeida et al. 2017;Cherepovitsyn and Lebedev 2023). 

Although prior studies have addressed specific aspects of drilling waste management, there is a notable scarcity of integrated reviews that link the technical complexities of drilling with the quantitative characterization and valorization of drill cuttings. This article aims to address this knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive view, from waste generation to potential reuse. This review is organized into the following topics: (1) Types of oil well drilling; (2) Drilling fluids; (3) Toxicity of drilling fluids; (4) Characterization methods of drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids; (5) Risk assessment; (6) Treatment technologies for drill cuttings management; (7) Valorization of drill cuttings; (8) Case studies and pilot-scale trials (9) Innovative advances in treatment; and (9) Legal aspects. This work is of particular importance in stimulating discussion and providing a foundational reference for those developing or implementing strategies for drill cutting management, thereby supporting more sustainable practices in the oil industry.

Title: Study on the effect of innovative leaching solvent on the oil removal for oily drilling cuttings
Snippet: A new type of leaching solvent for oily drilling cuttings was developed, and the effect of leaching solvent on the oil removal for oily cuttings was investigated. The results indicated that the leaching solvent had good capacity of oil removal for oily cuttings, and the oil content of treated cuttings is less than 0.6%. The leaching solvent could be separated from the oil phase through distillation, and the recyclable solvent could be reused to treat other cuttings. Moreover, oil resources adsorbed on the oily cuttings could be recycled and reused to prepare new drilling fluids, so the drilling cost could be reduced greatly. As a result, the leaching solvent could treat the oily cuttings effectively, and recycle and reuse oil resources, and thus produce great economic benefits. It can play an essential role in safe drilling jobs and improvement of drilling efficiency in the future.

Title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
Snippet: Extraction with supercritical fluids is a thermochemical separation process in which H 2 O and CO 2 are subjected to pressures and temperatures that cause their dielectric constants to decrease, and the solubility of both becomes similar to that of organic solvents (Radfarnia et al. 2015;Hu et al. 2022). When used for the extraction of oily fluids from drill cuttings, it was possible to extract up to 49% of the oily fluid from the drill cuttings using a pressure of 200 bar and a flow rate of 56.02 cm 3 /s of CO 2 (Goodarznia and Esmaeilzadeh 2006). However, this process is still little reported for the Fig. 5 Treatment options and potential reuse for drill cuttings treatment of drill cuttings, being more commonly used in the treatment of oily sludge (Pereira et al. 2022). 

When it comes to thermal processes, the most used ways for separating drill cuttings from fluids by using temperature are pyrolysis and microwave heating. Pyrolysis occurs through endo and exothermic processes, with stages of heating, vaporization, and cracking of the hydrocarbons adhered to the drill cuttings (Xu et al. 2023;Wang et al. 2024d). After the molecules broken, they are desorbed, reducing the oil content present in the drill cuttings. At the end, the small desorbed molecular fragments can be rearranged and resynthesized into petroleum hydrocarbons for the recovery and reuse of the oily fluid (Xu et al. 2023). This decontamination process is widely studied since it does not generate secondary pollutants, and the products (solids, liquids, and gases) can be recovered for reuse (Hou et al. 2018). Liu et al. (2023a), when evaluating the pyrolysis process in drill cuttings, achieved a reduction from 8.03% to 1.87% of oily fluid in the drill cuttings. They also observed that a recovery rate of over 98% of the oil could be obtained in residence times greater than 50 min and at temperatures above 350 °C.

Title: Novel Assessment of Drill Cuttings in Ionic Liquid
Snippet: The drill cuttings management process has consistently been reviewed to identify safer treatment methods that reduce environmental impact while improving recovery of residual chemicals to enable the reuse of the oil-free cuttings. Recycling and disposal are key waste management options that are of concern to the oil and gas industry. As significant quantities of drill cuttings are produced during drilling operations, there is an increased need for drill cuttings management solutions. This study investigates the novel use of ionic liquids to separate drilling fluid from cuttings. The findings from the laboratory research showed that the drilling fluid on the cuttings can be separated from the cuttings with the recovery of the extraction solvent for reuse in the recovery process. This approach emphasises the potential of ionic liquids in an integrated waste management approach to enhance material recovery.

Pyrolysis occurs through endo and exothermic processes, with stages of heating, vaporization, and cracking of the hydrocarbons adhered to the drill cuttings (Xu et al. 2023;Wang et al. 2024d). After the molecules broken, they are desorbed, reducing the oil content present in the drill cuttings. At the end, the small desorbed molecular fragments can be rearranged and resynthesized into petroleum hydrocarbons for the recovery and reuse of the oily fluid (Xu et al. 2023). This decontamination process is widely studied since it does not generate secondary pollutants, and the products (solids, liquids, and gases) can be recovered for reuse (Hou et al. 2018). Liu et al. (2023a), when evaluating the pyrolysis process in drill cuttings, achieved a reduction from 8.03% to 1.87% of oily fluid in the drill cuttings. They also observed that a recovery rate of over 98% of the oil could be obtained in residence times greater than 50 min and at temperatures above 350 °C.

documents.title: Novel Assessment of Drill Cuttings in Ionic Liquid
documents.snippet: The drill cuttings management process has consistently been reviewed to identify safer treatment methods that reduce environmental impact while improving recovery of residual chemicals to enable the reuse of the oil-free cuttings. Recycling and disposal are key waste management options that are of concern to the oil and gas industry. As significant quantities of drill cuttings are produced during drilling operations, there is an increased need for drill cuttings management solutions. This study investigates the novel use of ionic liquids to separate drilling fluid from cuttings. The findings from the laboratory research showed that the drilling fluid on the cuttings can be separated from the cuttings with the recovery of the extraction solvent for reuse in the recovery process. This approach emphasises the potential of ionic liquids in an integrated waste management approach to enhance material recovery.

Title: Recovery of Copper, Nickel and Zinc from Sulfate Solutions by Solvent Extraction Using LIX 984N
Snippet: Chalcopyrites, pentaldite, spent catalyst, batteries, brass ash, zinc ash are some of the major sources for the production of copper, nickel and zinc 1 . Apart from sulfides, significant resources for these metals are available as oxide/silicate deposits. These raw materials are subjected to various hydrometallurgical treatments which include atmospheric/pressure/bioleaching of sulfate/chloride solutions. The leach liquor, thus obtained contains copper, nickel, zinc along with some impurities such as iron, chromium, aluminium, silicon etc. Liquid-liquid extraction has been applied to many solutions to obtain either metals or their salts in highly pure form, as these metals are industrially and economically more important and therefore there is a great need to separate and recover them. Solvent extraction has been carried out extensively for the separation of cobalt and nickel with alkyl phosphorus reagents like Cyanex 272 and D2EHPA 2,3 . Similarly Chelating reagents like LIX 87QN, LIX 54, LIX 973, LIX 34, LIX 984, LIX 984N and LIX 84I have been used for the extraction, separation and recovery of copper, nickel and zinc from ammonium carbonate / ammonium sulfate solutions [4][5][6][7][8][9][10] . Extraction of copper, nickel and zinc from their sulfate solutions, using LIX 84I was found to depend on the equilibrium pH of the aqueous phase 11,12 . It was found that LIX 984N was very selective for copper extraction. In this paper, we report the solvent extraction separation of copper, nickel and zinc from synthetic solution using LIX 984 N as the extractant dissolved in kerosene, with an aim to separate these metals efficiently by single stage extraction. On the basis of this, a flow sheet of the process has been developed.

Summary: Highest-value valorization pathway
- Bottom line: Reuse of pre‑treated water‑based drill cuttings as raw materials in cement/concrete ranks as the highest‑value pathway today, ahead of ceramics and raw soil amendment, based on demonstrated technical feasibility across a wide scale, compliance‑oriented performance metrics (strength, leachability), and established industrial practices in construction supply chains, with ceramics offering viable alternatives at lower replacement levels and with mineralogical fit, and agricultural amendment offering niche but constrained benefits due to contaminant risks unless combined with robust pre‑treatment and monitoring. <cite id="3ef688bc-1">Reports show that pre‑treated drill cuttings can replace part of cement or fine aggregate in concrete, with compliance testing required for contaminants</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-2">and quantitative studies show 5–20% cement replacement yields 26–22 MPa at 28 days with acceptable leachability</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Valorization for civil construction is a major reuse stream pursued alongside environmental applications</cite>. <cite id="00291047-1">Ceramics can incorporate drill cuttings (e.g., bricks/ blocks) at certain concentrations and firing temperatures</cite> <cite id="00291047-3">with up to 40% clay replacement reported in red ceramics</cite>, while <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">soil amendment potential exists but requires purification when drilling fluids contain excessive heavy metals</cite>.

Background: What “water‑based” drill cuttings are and why valorization matters
- Water‑based drill cuttings are generated when water‑in‑oil or water‑based muds are used; the solids (e.g., barite, clay, carbonates) are recovered as slurry, while additives (biocides, corrosion inhibitors, lubricants) impart organics and trace metals. <cite id="8dfe77d0-4">Drilling wastes comprise used drilling fluids and cuttings; fluid phase can be water or oil/air/gas mixtures</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings commonly contain calcite, quartz, muscovite, dolomite, barite, and can include sylvite and orthoclase; drilling fluids may contain barium chloride</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">They are relatively rich in Ca, Mg, K and some trace elements essential for plants, but drilling fluids and some cuttings can exceed EC/PL limits for toxic metals (e.g., Ni, Hg, Pb), requiring purification before reuse</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Global reviews emphasize treatment/valorization pipelines from generation to reuse, with civil construction and environmental functions (e.g., adsorbents) highlighted</cite>.

Pathway 1 — Cement/concrete: technical performance and regulatory compliance
- Mechanically viable substitutions: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">A study replacing 5–25% cement (1:1.5:3 mix; w/b=0.5) with thermally treated drill cuttings achieved 26.20 N/mm² (5% replacement) to 22.46 N/mm² (20% replacement) at 28 days, exceeding minimums for C/20–C/25 classes; strength activity indices of 90.6–98.8% at 28 days surpassed the 75% code minimum</cite>. <cite id="3ef688bc-3">Treated drill cuttings met ASTM C618 pozzolan criteria (SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃≥70%) and improved mortar strength at 10–20% cement replacement across 7, 14, and 28 days</cite>. 
- Durability and leaching: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Durability under wet/dry cycles remained intact (less than 5% loss of structural integrity), and chloride and total PAH leachability met target values for reusable materials; activation at 500 °C for 180 min enhanced pozzolanic activity</cite>. 
- Microstructure and contaminants: <cite id="3ef688bc-0">In S/S matrices with 0–10% cuttings replacing fine aggregate (0.6–0.8 w/c; 1:2:4 mix), 2% addition yielded UCS of 22.22–26.22 N/mm² (>20 N/mm² threshold), but residual TPH in the stabilized matrix averaged 62.41 mg/kg, slightly above a local target of 50 mg/kg, indicating incomplete hydrocarbon immobilization and the need for contaminant screening</cite>. 
- Practical reuse patterns and quality control: <cite id="3ef688bc-1">Reviews note that pre‑treated cuttings can substitute for cement or sand in concrete, with compliance to environmental guidelines for contaminants enforced through analysis of the resulting concrete; conventional contaminant analyses are time‑ and cost‑intensive</cite>. 
- Value drivers: cement/concrete integration aligns with mature, high‑throughput construction markets; substitution fractions are evidence‑bounded (≤20% cement; ≤8–10% sand), with compliance testing and thermal pretreatment adding value via waste diversion and cost offsets for aggregates, while delivering comparable structural performance and documented durability. <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Civil construction reuse is a primary, widely considered valorization route</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-2">with quantified strength and leachability compliance at 5–20% cement replacement</cite>.

Pathway 2 — Ceramic manufacturing: mineralogical fit, replacement ranges, and performance
- Mineralogical compatibility: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings contain calcite, quartz, muscovite, dolomite, barite; drilling fluid residues can include sylvite and barium chloride</cite>. These phases are typical of ceramic raw mixes; carbonates and quartz act as fluxing/porosity‑generating components upon firing, aligning with practices that use carbonaceous additives to create lightweight, porous ceramics. <cite id="00291047-0">Pyrolysis of oil‑based drill cuttings can burn off organics, immobilize metals in crystals upon sintering, and, when combined with cement solidification, yields solid blocks; however, environmental pollution persists absent further processing, motivating conversion routes like sintering to valorize fractions</cite>. 
- Performance across formulations and firing: <cite id="00291047-1">Formulations with 0–100 wt% cuttings in a clay matrix fired 850–1050 °C produced solid masonry bricks and blocks meeting technological property targets at certain concentrations and temperatures</cite>. <cite id="00291047-3">Replacing up to 40% of clay in red ceramic bodies with waste drilling fluid/cuttings enabled tiles, massive and hollow bricks meeting normative requirements for technological properties</cite>. <cite id="00291047-4">Incorporating drilling sludge (≈10% of ceramic mass) produced lightweight class B bricks by creating fired‑on porosity; increasing to 20% raised efficiency class, effectively partially replacing brown coal as a pore‑forming fuel</cite>. 
- Value drivers and constraints: Ceramics can absorb lower fractions (10–40% clay replacement) with acceptable mechanical and technological properties when properly formulated and fired, leveraging local clay supply chains; however, the presence of chlorinated additives (e.g., biocides) and variable organic load demands pretreatment (e.g., pyrolysis, thermal desorption) to avoid bloating, discoloration, or atmospheric emissions during firing. <cite id="00291047-0">Sintering can burn off oil and lock in heavy metals in crystals, improving material quality</cite> <cite id="00291047-1">with viability contingent on concentration and firing temperature windows</cite>.

Pathway 3 — Agricultural soil amendment: nutrients, risks, and remediation
- Nutrient and mineral inputs: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings are relatively rich in Ca, Mg, K and trace elements (Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, Al, Cr, Ni, Pb), with mineralogies including calcite, quartz, muscovite, sylvite, dolomite, barite, and barium chloride</cite>, supporting roles in soil conditioning and land reclamation when purified. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Spent drilling fluids can contain excessive Ni, Hg, and Pb; one drilling fluid sample had 270 mg/kg Ni (exceeding 75 mg/kg EC limit) and 8.77 mg/kg Hg (vs 1.5 mg/kg EC), and a cuttings sample had 250 mg/kg Pb (vs 200 mg/kg PL limit), necessitating purification before use</cite>. 
- Reuse contexts and bioremediation: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Solid wastes (drilling fluids and cuttings) if properly treated can serve as raw materials for soil amendment production, useful for land reclamation of well sites, mining sites, and contaminated lands</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">Biological treatments (e.g., composting with PAH‑degrading mycelium) can transform contaminated drill cuttings into marketable soil conditioners and organic fertilizers, reducing environmental risks</cite>. 
- Value drivers and constraints: Agronomic valorization can deliver soil structure and nutrient benefits at sites requiring reclamation or organic matter, but risk management requires washing, thermal desorption, or composting/biostabilization to meet soil quality standards; regulatory acceptance hinges on leaching limits for metals and PAHs and on site‑specific remediation goals. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">High levels of toxic elements in some cuttings/drilling fluids require purification before agricultural or environmental reuse</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Valorization in agriculture is one of several reuse options pursued in comprehensive management frameworks</cite>.

Comparative assessment: Why cement/concrete is currently highest‑value
- Scale and integration: <cite id="8dfe77d0-4">Drilling wastes are among the second largest wastes from E&P, motivating mature management options such as land application and civil construction reuse</cite>. The cement/concrete value chain is mature and standardized, with clear acceptance criteria for contaminant leaching and mechanical performance, enabling deployment of pre‑treated cuttings as supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) or fine aggregates. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Evidence shows 5–20% cement replacement yields 26–22 MPa at 28 days with acceptable chloride/PAH leachability</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-1">and compliance testing integrated into reuse protocols</cite>. 
- Performance/quality: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Compressive strengths exceed or match structural classes C/20–C/25 with 5–20% replacement and improved durability under wet/dry cycling</cite>; <cite id="3ef688bc-0">2% fine‑aggregate replacement in cement‑based matrices achieved UCS ≥22.22 N/mm²</cite>. These metrics, combined with <cite id="3ef688bc-3">ASTM C618‑level pozzolanic reactivity</cite>, underpin higher‑value circularity claims than landfill diversion or unprocessed spreading. 
- Risk control tractability: Heavy metals and organics are manageable through thermal/bio‑pretreatment and S/S verification, with <cite id="3ef688bc-0">residual TPH 62.41 mg/kg indicating the need for stricter hydrocarbon targets or additional steps</cite>, but protocols exist; this yields higher residual value than raw soil application where risk can exceed benefit without rigorous purification. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">High Hg, Ni, and Pb levels in some samples necessitate purification for soil reuse</cite>. 
- Relative standing of ceramics and soil amendment: <cite id="00291047-1">Ceramics can use drill cuttings at viable concentrations and temperatures for bricks/blocks</cite> and <cite id="00291047-3">up to 40% clay replacement in red ceramics</cite>, offering material performance and cost benefits for lightweighting and local brick/tile markets, but often at lower substitution fractions and with stricter formulation/firing controls than cement blending. <cite id="00291047-4">Organic matter in cuttings acts as burnable pore‑formers to produce lightweight class B bricks, with higher efficiency at 20% loading</cite>. For soil, benefits exist but are geographically specific and risk‑constrained; <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">nutrient content is positive, yet regulatory limits are easily exceeded without purification</cite>, and <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">bioremediation pathways can convert cuttings into soil conditioners</cite>. 

When is the ranking reversed or hybridized?
- If the site context is post‑drilling reclamation or degraded farmland with demonstrated need for organic matter and micronutrients, and if high‑risk cuttings are unavailable or affordably purified, agricultural soil amendment can be a high‑value, restorative pathway. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Soil amendments from treated cuttings have been proposed for site revitalization and land reclamation</cite>. 
- For low‑to‑moderate strength masonry and lightweight block supply, ceramics can offer higher local value where raw materials are expensive; <cite id="00291047-1">0–100 wt% cuttings can be viable at specific temperatures</cite> and <cite id="00291047-3">40% clay replacement in red ceramics</cite> can reduce costs and curb emissions during firing via pore‑forming effects, though organic/biocide management remains critical. <cite id="00291047-0">Sintering routes address oil and metal immobilization</cite>.

Practical recommendations to maximize value and minimize risk
- Cement/concrete reuse: 
  - Target 5–20% cement replacement with 1:1.5:3 or equivalent mixes and w/b≈0.5; verify 28‑day strength and leachability for metals and PAHs; consider 500 °C activation of treated cuttings to enhance pozzolanic reactivity. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">5–25% cement replacement achieved 26.20–22.46 MPa with acceptable leachability</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-3">and ASTM C618 compliance with 10–20% replacement</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-0">with microstructure confirming strength gains</cite>. 
  - Use pretreatments that reduce TPH below regulatory targets; where necessary, supplement S/S with additional stabilization or adjust w/c and curing. <cite id="3ef688bc-0">Residual TPH 62.41 mg/kg exceeded a 50 mg/kg target</cite>. 
- Ceramic reuse: 
  - Start with 5–15% loading in standard red/mortar clays, expand to 20–40% where local clays are scarce and firing schedules are tuned; incorporate pyrolysis/bio‑oxidation to remove organics and immobilize metals in crystalline phases. <cite id="00291047-1">Formulations 0–100 wt% cuttings with 850–1050 °C firing yielded viable bricks/blocks at specific windows</cite> <cite id="00291047-3">40% clay replacement met requirements</cite> <cite id="00291047-0">sintering converts organics and locks in metals</cite>. 
- Soil amendment: 
  - Apply only to contaminated or degraded lands needing organic matter; enforce washing/thermal/bio‑remediation to meet metal and PAH leaching limits; integrate with composting/mushroom‑compost biostabilization for hydrocarbon degradation. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Purification is required when Hg, Ni, Pb exceed limits</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">composting with PAH‑degrading mycelium produces soil conditioners and organic fertilizers</cite>. 

Evidence gaps and how to resolve them
- Direct head‑to‑head cost/GHG footprints across cement, ceramics, and soil pathways are not consistently quantified in accessible studies; however, construction reuse aligns with accepted compliance frameworks and demonstrated performance, whereas soil reuse is constrained by contaminant risk unless treated. Future work should conduct cradle‑to‑gate GHG and techno‑economic analyses benchmarking: (a) cement/concrete (SCM vs. baseline), (b) ceramic tiles/bricks with cuttings vs. virgin bodies, and (c) agronomic yield responses and metal/PAH leaching under field conditions, with sensitivity to pretreatment energy/cost. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Demonstrated leachability compliance and strength</cite> <cite id="00291047-1">technological viability in ceramics</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">and regulatory constraints for soil</cite> provide anchors for such comparative assessments. 

Bottom line for your three options:
- Highest‑value: Cement/concrete integration of pre‑treated water‑based drill cuttings, given scalable value chains, evidence‑bounded performance (≥20 MPa at 5–20% cement replacement), compliance‑oriented durability and leachability, and accepted risk management via pretreatment. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">5–20% cement replacement achieved 26–22 MPa with acceptable durability and leachability</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-1">with reuse protocols tied to regulatory compliance</cite>.

- Context‑dependent niche: Agricultural soil amendment where land remediation/organic matter needs exceed, with high‑risk cuttings supplied via washing/thermal/bio‑remediation to meet soil standards. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Nutrient and mineral inputs are beneficial but metal/PAH constraints require purification</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">biological composting can turn cuttings into soil conditioners and fertilizers</cite>.

Title: Environmental aspects of drill cuttings from oil operations: characterization, risk assessment, valorization, and treatment innovations
Snippet: The decontaminated drill cutting can be used in civil construction or can be repurposed in the environmental sector as adsorbents or catalysts for removing pollutants from wastewater (Yang et al. 2022a). Additionally, there is an opportunity to implement global-scale treatment and valorization solutions for drill cuttings contaminated (de Almeida et al. 2017;Cherepovitsyn and Lebedev 2023). 

Although prior studies have addressed specific aspects of drilling waste management, there is a notable scarcity of integrated reviews that link the technical complexities of drilling with the quantitative characterization and valorization of drill cuttings. This article aims to address this knowledge gap by offering a comprehensive view, from waste generation to potential reuse. This review is organized into the following topics: (1) Types of oil well drilling; (2) Drilling fluids; (3) Toxicity of drilling fluids; (4) Characterization methods of drill cuttings contaminated with drilling fluids; (5) Risk assessment; (6) Treatment technologies for drill cuttings management; (7) Valorization of drill cuttings; (8) Case studies and pilot-scale trials (9) Innovative advances in treatment; and (9) Legal aspects. Title: The application of composting materials to degrade polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon on oil field drill cuttings
Snippet: A substantial volume of oily sludge is generated during oil production and processing activities, with oil and gas drilling operations worldwide producing drill-cutting wastes. Managing fossil fuel waste has become a prominent topic in the environmental industry in recent years. Historically, these drill cuttings were often disposed of in water bodies or on land without any prior treatment (Browning and Seaton, 2005). Additionally, companies engaged in burning fossil fuels commonly stockpiled waste, either relocating it or burying the drill cuttings, thereby exacerbating contamination risks. 

Most fossil fuel waste, specifically drill cuttings, contains a considerable amount of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which serve as a potent energy source for mycelium (spent mushroom compost). Drill cuttings have been characterized by a relatively high content of PAHs (DPR, 2002) and heavy metals (Khajiagbe et al., 2014). Over the years, various methods, including thermal treatment technologies, solidification/stabilization (Shaffer et al., 1998;Allagoa, 2014), and mechanochemistry (Peng et al., 2018), have been employed for the management of drill cuttings. 

Since the 1970s, biological treatments have been actively utilized for hydrocarbon degradation and are now considered among the most effective cleanup alternatives for soil (Kuppusamy et al., 2017). Composting, as an exsitu bioremediation technology, is particularly adept at treating large volumes of polluted soils. It plays a crucial role in the sustainable recycling of organic waste (Fermor, 1993;Tuomela et al., 2000;Andrew et al., 1999;Hachicha et al., 2009;Greenway and Song, 2002) and results in a marketable end product used as a soil conditioner and organic fertilizer. 

The addition of organic waste is essential to promote the development of a diverse microbial community capable of breaking down complex contaminants (Aitken et al., 1992;Jorgensen et al., 2000;Ma et al., 2016). A case study on Mushroom compost-assisted remediation of soil contaminated with PAHs from a manufactured gas plant was conducted in a thermally insulated composting chamber.
</snippet>

Title: Towards enhancing sustainable reuse of pre-treated drill cuttings for construction purposes by near-infrared analysis: A review
Snippet: The predictable generation of drill cuttings during crude oil drilling activities has in recent times become one of the major global environmental concerns because of the hazardous nature of the drilling waste. Until recently, untreated drill cuttings were dumped into the seabed and on land during off-shore and land-based crude oil drilling operations respectively. From innumerable sources, records show staggering negative impacts of sea and land disposal of untreated drill cuttings on benthic and edaphic fauna and flora. Currently, various treatment technologies are available for drill cuttings; a majority of which is driven largely by the intention to either recover the solid components for possible land application for agricultural purposes (Kogbara et al., 2017) or reuse them for civil engineering works (International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP), 2016). 

One of the tenets of sustainable reuse of hazardous wastes like drill cuttings in civil engineering works like concrete production is to ensure that the resulting concrete complies with environmental guidelines. These guidelines are intended to protect ecological health well into the future. Available records show that drill cuttings *Corresponding author. Author(s) agree that this article remain permanently open access under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License 4.0 International License are heavily laden with heavy metals and hydrocarbons (Ayotamuno et al., 2007;Okparanma et al., 2007). Even when drill cuttings have been thermally pre-treated, some of these contaminants remain (IOGP, 2016). Reports also show that pre-treated drill cuttings could be reused as part substitute for cement or fine aggregate in concrete (IOGP, 2016). In keeping with the tenets of sustainable reuse of hazardous wastes like drill cuttings, the resulting concrete is first analyzed for residual contaminants before it is put to the intended use. 

However, issues remain particularly with the conventional concrete characterization techniques, which include crushing, acid digestion, solvent extraction, and instrumental analysis. These issues include costly delays due to lengthy sample preparation protocols, occupational health concerns associated with the use of noxious extraction solvents, and high analytical costs.

Title: An assessment of the effectiveness of drilling waste treatment process in X-gas field, Niger Delta, Nigeria
Snippet: Previously, waste materials generated from various activities related to oil and gas exploration, production, storage, and transportation were regarded as useless, unwanted, and unusable and therefore were usually discarded. With recent developments in recycling and resource recovery technologies, the concept of waste management has changed. Materials previously regarded as useless and unwanted are now treated and reprocessed into various valuable or safer products. Drilling wastes are wastes generated during drilling of oil, gas, or water; and they are classified as used drilling fluids and drill cuttings (DCs). Drilling fluids (muds) lubricate and cool the bits, aid in lifting the drilling cuttings to the surface, control the formation pressures, and allow good drilling performance (Cordah, 1998;Davies & Kingston, 1992). The fluid phase of drilling mud can be water or mixture of natural oils, air, and gas (Onwukwe & Nwakaudu, 2012). 

Drilling wastes make up to the second largest of the total volume of wastes generated by the exploration and production industry aside produced water (DOE, 1999;Haut, Rogers, McDole, Burnett, & Olatubi, 2007). Onshore operations have a wider range of management options than offshore operations. Proper management of drilling wastes should be considered especially in the areas where its toxic constituents could easily leach into the soil, surface, and groundwater systems. The pollution associated with drilling fluid wastes are caused by biocides, oil, completion or stimulation fluid components, corrosion inhibitors, reservoir fluids, and chemical component of drilling fluids (Patin, 2004). Wastes generated during drilling also have potential to impact on the soil quality, health, water, and entire ecosystem negatively if not properly managed (Sherif et al., 2017). 

Drilling waste management is a means of controlling, collection, storage, transportation, processing, and disposal of wastes generated during drilling in a safe and acceptable environment that is in context with the existing regulatory requirements. Various management options, such as land application, underground injection, thermal treatment, and biological processes, can be used for drilling wastes remediation (Furukawa, Mukai, & Ohmura, 2017). 

Drilling waste contains organic, inorganic, and heavy elements.

Title: Diagnostic screening of organic contaminant level in solidified/stabilized pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings
Snippet: The reuse of solidified/stabilized low-temperature thermally desorbed (pre-treated) oil-based drill cuttings for construction purposes is becoming increasingly attractive in recent times; though, without screening a priori the levels of target residual organic contaminants against environmental guidelines to ensure compliance. In this study, pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings were collected from a waste treatment facility in the Niger Delta Province (5.317oN; 6.467oE), Nigeria and subjected to cement-based solidification/stabilization (S/S) followed by chemical leaching and screening of the data against local environmental guidelines. S/S was done with drill cuttings contents of 0 (control), 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 % as part replacement for fine aggregate at 0.6:1, 0.65:1, 0.7:1, 0.75:1, and 0.8:1 water-to-cement ratios using 1:2:4 mix design for a grade-20 concrete. Afterwards, the surface microstructure, elemental composition, and unconfined compressive strength (UCS) of the solidified/stabilized matrix were determined. Amounts of heavy metals and total petroleum hydrocarbons (TPH) leached were also assessed. Results showed that the 2 % drill cuttings addition yielded the highest UCS (22.22–26.22 N/mm2) at water-to-cement ratio of 0.6:1, which were well above the recommended minimum UCS of 20 N/mm2 for a grade-20 concrete. The average amount of residual TPH in the solidified/stabilized matrix (62.41 mg/kg) was slightly higher than the local regulatory target value of 50 mg/kg; suggesting that the cement-based S/S failed to immobilize completely all the hydrocarbons in the pre-treated oil-based drill cuttings. This shows that the solidified/stabilized matrix is not in compliance with environmental guidelines on TPH for sustainable reuse as construction materials.
</snippet>

Title: Towards enhancing sustainable reuse of pre-treated drill cuttings for construction purposes by near-infrared analysis: A review
Snippet: The predictable generation of drill cuttings during crude oil drilling activities has in recent times become one of the major global environmental concerns because of the hazardous nature of the drilling waste. Until recently, untreated drill cuttings were dumped into the seabed and on land during off-shore and land-based crude oil drilling operations respectively. From innumerable sources, records show staggering negative impacts of sea and land disposal of untreated drill cuttings on benthic and edaphic fauna and flora. Currently, various treatment technologies are available for drill cuttings; a majority of which is driven largely by the intention to either recover the solid components for possible land application for agricultural purposes (Kogbara et al., 2017) or reuse them for civil engineering works (International Association of Oil and Gas Producers (IOGP), 2016). 

One of the tenets of sustainable reuse of hazardous wastes like drill cuttings in civil engineering works like concrete production is to ensure that the resulting concrete complies with environmental guidelines. These guidelines are intended to protect ecological health well into the future. Available records show that drill cuttings *Corresponding author. However, issues remain particularly with the conventional concrete characterization techniques, which include crushing, acid digestion, solvent extraction, and instrumental analysis. These issues include costly delays due to lengthy sample preparation protocols, occupational health concerns associated with the use of noxious extraction solvents, and high analytical costs.

Title: Compressive strength and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production
Snippet: This study examines the compressive strengths and leachability effects of treated drill cuttings as a partial replacement of cement in concrete production. Workability tests on various water-binder ratios (w/b) on the fresh concrete showed that an optimum w/b of 0.5 was adequate for the concrete to be workable. Replacement levels of 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25% were used to produce cement-drill cuttings concrete at a 1:1.5:3 mix ratio. The blended concrete gave a compressive strength in the range of 26.20N/mm 2 for 5% to 22.46N/mm 2 for 20% replacement levels at 28 days curing time, more than the minimum compressive strength of 20N/mm 2 and 25N/mm 2 specified for concrete strength class C/20 and C/25, respectively. The strength activity index of 90.56, 98.76, 89.05, 98.05, and 77.64% for 5, 10, 15, and 20% replacement levels at 28 days of curing time was obtained surpassing the minimum 75% specified for normal concrete by the code. The wet/dry durability effects of the blended concrete at any replacement level passed the structural integrity with less than 5% of the structural integrity of the material lost. The chloride and total polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (TPAHs) leachability effects both met the DPRs target values for reusable materials. The study has shown that drill cuttings have a good pozzolanic effect on concrete, especially when activated at the temperature of 500oC for 180 minutes. It also shows that treated drill cuttings could replace cement up to 20% by weight to produce concrete of adequate strength using a w/b ratio of 0.5 and mix ratios of 1:1.5:3. The study has also shown that treated drill cuttings replaced with cement to produce concrete which is durable to both wet/dry and leaching effects of chlorides and TPAHs to the environment.
</snippet>

Title: The Use of Drill Cuttings as Pozzolan for Concrete Production
Snippet: This study was carried out to determine the pozzolanic potential of treated drill cuttings in the production of mortar and the effect of incorporating pozzolanic materials (treated drill cuttings) with ordinary portland cement on the properties of cement, mortar and concrete with the following conclusions drawn: 

The physical and chemical oxide tests on the samples indicated that the treated drill cuttings meet the requirements for a pozzolan for use in the production of blended cements. 

The combined chemical oxide mix composition (i.e. SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃) of the treated drill cuttings demonstrated that the treated drill cuttings satisfied the criteria for pozzolans as stipulated by ASTM C618 (ASTM 2003), which requires a minimum sum of 70% for the three main oxides (SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃). 

The results of the compressive strength confirmed that the strength enhancements of mortar are achievable with partial replacement of cement with treated drill cuttings. The strength of pozzolanic cement is higher than that of control mortar (0% treated drill cuttings addition) at 10% and 20% replacements of cement at ages 7, 14, and 28 days. 

This study therefore concludes that, the compressive strength of the treated drill cuttings-cement blended mortar is adequate for sandcrete block production with improved properties and usage in construction, using 1:3 mix ratios with a water/binder ratio of 0.40:1. Thus demonstrating the potential for the beneficial reuse of oil drill cuttings treated by thermal desorption, as partial replacement of cement for the production of sandcrete blocks.
</snippet>

Title: Manufacturing of ceramic lightweight aggregates from oil-based drill cutting pyrolysis residues
Snippet: As a new energy resource, shale gas exploration and development cause high environmental risks as approximately 250 m 3 of oil-based drill cuttings are generated by one well [1]. Pyrolysis is typically performed for oily solid wastes to maintain the oil content within 0.3% and facilitate a solidification process [2]. After the solidification with cement, the absolute majority of contaminants in drill cutting pyrolysis residues (DCPR) form solidified blocks [3][4][5][6]; however, it does not mitigate the pollution caused by oil and heavy metals. By conducting a sintering process, oil can be burned while heavy metals become solidified in crystals. 

High-quality kaolin, bauxites, and refractory clays are natural raw materials traditionally used for the production of aluminosilicate ceramic proppants [7,8], while natural and artificial additives are utilized to promote the sintering process and increase the strength of the final product [9][10][11][12][13][14][15]. However, owing to the scarcity and gradual depletion of high-quality clays and kaolin, low-grade clays (so-called brick clays) are widely used for the preparation of LWAs [16,17]. It is well known that the mechanical strength of ceramics primarily depends on their crystal structure [18], phase composition [19], and sintering characteristics (density and porosity) [20]. Previous studies describing the use of certain igneous rocks, such as basalt rocks [21][22][23], granites, and diabase [24][25][26], in ceramic brick technology have confirmed their effects by increasing the total content of the crystalline phase. For example, Jiang et al. [27] reported that the leaching rate of aluminabased ceramic core materials containing silica fibers was relatively high. 

According to the GB/T 17431.2-2010 standard [28], in addition to high compressive strength (above 3.6 MPa), LWAs should also possess sufficiently small particle and bulk densities (below 1200 kg/m 3 ).
</snippet>

Title: Study on the Viability of Using Drill Cuttings from the Potiguar Basin in the Production of Ceramic Products: Influence of Concentration and Firing Temperature
Snippet: Drill cuttings are wastes produced on a large scale during the drilling of oil wells. Although there are several treatment techniques, there is still no consensus on which one are the best for the economy and environmental. On the other hand, one of the alternatives for the reuse of this waste, and purpose of the present study, is the incorporation of drill cuttings in clay matrixes. The raw materials used in this work, a mixture of clays and drill cuttings, were investigated by two basic techniques of characterization. X-ray fluorescence and X-ray diffraction. In order to evaluate the effect of the content of drill cuttings on the technological properties of sintered ceramics, different formulations containing from 0 wt.% to 100 wt.% of drill cuttings in a clay matrix were obtained. Ceramic samples were obtained by firing at temperatures ranging from 850 °C to 1050 °C. The fired specimens were characterized by water absorption, firing linear shrinkage, resistance to bending three points and scanning electron microscopy analysis. The results indicated that the incorporation of drill cuttings is a viable alternative for the manufacture of several ceramics products, such as solid masonry bricks and ceramic blocks, at certain concentrations and firing temperatures.
</snippet>

Summary: Highest-value valorization pathway
- Bottom line: Reuse of pre‑treated water‑based drill cuttings as raw materials in cement/concrete ranks as the highest‑value pathway today, ahead of ceramics and raw soil amendment, based on demonstrated technical feasibility across a wide scale, compliance‑oriented performance metrics (strength, leachability), and established industrial practices in construction supply chains, with ceramics offering viable alternatives at lower replacement levels and with mineralogical fit, and agricultural amendment offering niche but constrained benefits due to contaminant risks unless combined with robust pre‑treatment and monitoring. <cite id="3ef688bc-1">Reports show that pre‑treated drill cuttings can replace part of cement or fine aggregate in concrete, with compliance testing required for contaminants</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-2">and quantitative studies show 5–20% cement replacement yields 26–22 MPa at 28 days with acceptable leachability</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Valorization for civil construction is a major reuse stream pursued alongside environmental applications</cite>. <cite id="00291047-1">Ceramics can incorporate drill cuttings (e.g., bricks/ blocks) at certain concentrations and firing temperatures</cite> <cite id="00291047-3">with up to 40% clay replacement reported in red ceramics</cite>, while <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">soil amendment potential exists but requires purification when drilling fluids contain excessive heavy metals</cite>.

Background: What “water‑based” drill cuttings are and why valorization matters
- Water‑based drill cuttings are generated when water‑in‑oil or water‑based muds are used; the solids (e.g., barite, clay, carbonates) are recovered as slurry, while additives (biocides, corrosion inhibitors, lubricants) impart organics and trace metals. <cite id="8dfe77d0-4">Drilling wastes comprise used drilling fluids and cuttings; fluid phase can be water or oil/air/gas mixtures</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings commonly contain calcite, quartz, muscovite, dolomite, barite, and can include sylvite and orthoclase; drilling fluids may contain barium chloride</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">They are relatively rich in Ca, Mg, K and some trace elements essential for plants, but drilling fluids and some cuttings can exceed EC/PL limits for toxic metals (e.g., Ni, Hg, Pb), requiring purification before reuse</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Global reviews emphasize treatment/valorization pipelines from generation to reuse, with civil construction and environmental functions (e.g., adsorbents) highlighted</cite>.

Pathway 1 — Cement/concrete: technical performance and regulatory compliance
- Mechanically viable substitutions: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">A study replacing 5–25% cement (1:1.5:3 mix; w/b=0.5) with thermally treated drill cuttings achieved 26.20 N/mm² (5% replacement) to 22.46 N/mm² (20% replacement) at 28 days, exceeding minimums for C/20–C/25 classes; strength activity indices of 90.6–98.8% at 28 days surpassed the 75% code minimum</cite>. <cite id="3ef688bc-3">Treated drill cuttings met ASTM C618 pozzolan criteria (SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃≥70%) and improved mortar strength at 10–20% cement replacement across 7, 14, and 28 days</cite>. 
- Durability and leaching: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Durability under wet/dry cycles remained intact (less than 5% loss of structural integrity), and chloride and total PAH leachability met target values for reusable materials; activation at 500 °C for 180 min enhanced pozzolanic activity</cite>. 
- Microstructure and contaminants: <cite id="3ef688bc-0">In S/S matrices with 0–10% cuttings replacing fine aggregate (0.6–0.8 w/c; 1:2:4 mix), 2% addition yielded UCS of 22.22–26.22 N/mm² (>20 N/mm² threshold), but residual TPH in the stabilized matrix averaged 62.41 mg/kg, slightly above a local target of 50 mg/kg, indicating incomplete hydrocarbon immobilization and the need for contaminant screening</cite>. 
- Practical reuse patterns and quality control: <cite id="3ef688bc-1">Reviews note that pre‑treated cuttings can substitute for cement or sand in concrete, with compliance to environmental guidelines for contaminants enforced through analysis of the resulting concrete; conventional contaminant analyses are time‑ and cost‑intensive</cite>. 
- Value drivers: cement/concrete integration aligns with mature, high‑throughput construction markets; substitution fractions are evidence‑bounded (≤20% cement; ≤8–10% sand), with compliance testing and thermal pretreatment adding value via waste diversion and cost offsets for aggregates, while delivering comparable structural performance and documented durability. <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Civil construction reuse is a primary, widely considered valorization route</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-2">with quantified strength and leachability compliance at 5–20% cement replacement</cite>.

Pathway 2 — Ceramic manufacturing: mineralogical fit, replacement ranges, and performance
- Mineralogical compatibility: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings contain calcite, quartz, muscovite, dolomite, barite; drilling fluid residues can include sylvite and barium chloride</cite>. These phases are typical of ceramic raw mixes; carbonates and quartz act as fluxing/porosity‑generating components upon firing, aligning with practices that use carbonaceous additives to create lightweight, porous ceramics. <cite id="00291047-0">Pyrolysis of oil‑based drill cuttings can burn off organics, immobilize metals in crystals upon sintering, and, when combined with cement solidification, yields solid blocks; however, environmental pollution persists absent further processing, motivating conversion routes like sintering to valorize fractions</cite>. 
- Performance across formulations and firing: <cite id="00291047-1">Formulations with 0–100 wt% cuttings in a clay matrix fired 850–1050 °C produced solid masonry bricks and blocks meeting technological property targets at certain concentrations and temperatures</cite>. <cite id="00291047-3">Replacing up to 40% of clay in red ceramic bodies with waste drilling fluid/cuttings enabled tiles, massive and hollow bricks meeting normative requirements for technological properties</cite>. <cite id="00291047-4">Incorporating drilling sludge (≈10% of ceramic mass) produced lightweight class B bricks by creating fired‑on porosity; increasing to 20% raised efficiency class, effectively partially replacing brown coal as a pore‑forming fuel</cite>. 
- Value drivers and constraints: Ceramics can absorb lower fractions (10–40% clay replacement) with acceptable mechanical and technological properties when properly formulated and fired, leveraging local clay supply chains; however, the presence of chlorinated additives (e.g., biocides) and variable organic load demands pretreatment (e.g., pyrolysis, thermal desorption) to avoid bloating, discoloration, or atmospheric emissions during firing. <cite id="00291047-0">Sintering can burn off oil and lock in heavy metals in crystals, improving material quality</cite> <cite id="00291047-1">with viability contingent on concentration and firing temperature windows</cite>.

Pathway 3 — Agricultural soil amendment: nutrients, risks, and remediation
- Nutrient and mineral inputs: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Drill cuttings are relatively rich in Ca, Mg, K and trace elements (Cu, Fe, Mn, Zn, Al, Cr, Ni, Pb), with mineralogies including calcite, quartz, muscovite, sylvite, dolomite, barite, and barium chloride</cite>, supporting roles in soil conditioning and land reclamation when purified. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Spent drilling fluids can contain excessive Ni, Hg, and Pb; one drilling fluid sample had 270 mg/kg Ni (exceeding 75 mg/kg EC limit) and 8.77 mg/kg Hg (vs 1.5 mg/kg EC), and a cuttings sample had 250 mg/kg Pb (vs 200 mg/kg PL limit), necessitating purification before use</cite>. 
- Reuse contexts and bioremediation: <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Solid wastes (drilling fluids and cuttings) if properly treated can serve as raw materials for soil amendment production, useful for land reclamation of well sites, mining sites, and contaminated lands</cite>. <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">Biological treatments (e.g., composting with PAH‑degrading mycelium) can transform contaminated drill cuttings into marketable soil conditioners and organic fertilizers, reducing environmental risks</cite>. 
- Value drivers and constraints: Agronomic valorization can deliver soil structure and nutrient benefits at sites requiring reclamation or organic matter, but risk management requires washing, thermal desorption, or composting/biostabilization to meet soil quality standards; regulatory acceptance hinges on leaching limits for metals and PAHs and on site‑specific remediation goals. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">High levels of toxic elements in some cuttings/drilling fluids require purification before agricultural or environmental reuse</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-1">Valorization in agriculture is one of several reuse options pursued in comprehensive management frameworks</cite>.

Comparative assessment: Why cement/concrete is currently highest‑value
- Scale and integration: <cite id="8dfe77d0-4">Drilling wastes are among the second largest wastes from E&P, motivating mature management options such as land application and civil construction reuse</cite>. The cement/concrete value chain is mature and standardized, with clear acceptance criteria for contaminant leaching and mechanical performance, enabling deployment of pre‑treated cuttings as supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) or fine aggregates. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Evidence shows 5–20% cement replacement yields 26–22 MPa at 28 days with acceptable chloride/PAH leachability</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-1">and compliance testing integrated into reuse protocols</cite>. 
- Performance/quality: <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Compressive strengths exceed or match structural classes C/20–C/25 with 5–20% replacement and improved durability under wet/dry cycling</cite>; <cite id="3ef688bc-0">2% fine‑aggregate replacement in cement‑based matrices achieved UCS ≥22.22 N/mm²</cite>. These metrics, combined with <cite id="3ef688bc-3">ASTM C618‑level pozzolanic reactivity</cite>, underpin higher‑value circularity claims than landfill diversion or unprocessed spreading. 
- Risk control tractability: Heavy metals and organics are manageable through thermal/bio‑pretreatment and S/S verification, with <cite id="3ef688bc-0">residual TPH 62.41 mg/kg indicating the need for stricter hydrocarbon targets or additional steps</cite>, but protocols exist; this yields higher residual value than raw soil application where risk can exceed benefit without rigorous purification. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">High Hg, Ni, and Pb levels in some samples necessitate purification for soil reuse</cite>. 
- Relative standing of ceramics and soil amendment: <cite id="00291047-1">Ceramics can use drill cuttings at viable concentrations and temperatures for bricks/blocks</cite> and <cite id="00291047-3">up to 40% clay replacement in red ceramics</cite>, offering material performance and cost benefits for lightweighting and local brick/tile markets, but often at lower substitution fractions and with stricter formulation/firing controls than cement blending. <cite id="00291047-4">Organic matter in cuttings acts as burnable pore‑formers to produce lightweight class B bricks, with higher efficiency at 20% loading</cite>. For soil, benefits exist but are geographically specific and risk‑constrained; <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">nutrient content is positive, yet regulatory limits are easily exceeded without purification</cite>, and <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">bioremediation pathways can convert cuttings into soil conditioners</cite>. 

When is the ranking reversed or hybridized?
- If the site context is post‑drilling reclamation or degraded farmland with demonstrated need for organic matter and micronutrients, and if high‑risk cuttings are unavailable or affordably purified, agricultural soil amendment can be a high‑value, restorative pathway. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Soil amendments from treated cuttings have been proposed for site revitalization and land reclamation</cite>. 
- For low‑to‑moderate strength masonry and lightweight block supply, ceramics can offer higher local value where raw materials are expensive; <cite id="00291047-1">0–100 wt% cuttings can be viable at specific temperatures</cite> and <cite id="00291047-3">40% clay replacement in red ceramics</cite> can reduce costs and curb emissions during firing via pore‑forming effects, though organic/biocide management remains critical. <cite id="00291047-0">Sintering routes address oil and metal immobilization</cite>.

Practical recommendations to maximize value and minimize risk
- Cement/concrete reuse: 
  - Target 5–20% cement replacement with 1:1.5:3 or equivalent mixes and w/b≈0.5; verify 28‑day strength and leachability for metals and PAHs; consider 500 °C activation of treated cuttings to enhance pozzolanic reactivity. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">5–25% cement replacement achieved 26.20–22.46 MPa with acceptable leachability</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-3">and ASTM C618 compliance with 10–20% replacement</cite> <cite id="3ef688bc-0">with microstructure confirming strength gains</cite>. 
  - Use pretreatments that reduce TPH below regulatory targets; where necessary, supplement S/S with additional stabilization or adjust w/c and curing. <cite id="3ef688bc-0">Residual TPH 62.41 mg/kg exceeded a 50 mg/kg target</cite>. 
- Ceramic reuse: 
  - Start with 5–15% loading in standard red/mortar clays, expand to 20–40% where local clays are scarce and firing schedules are tuned; incorporate pyrolysis/bio‑oxidation to remove organics and immobilize metals in crystalline phases. <cite id="00291047-1">Formulations 0–100 wt% cuttings with 850–1050 °C firing yielded viable bricks/blocks at specific windows</cite> <cite id="00291047-3">40% clay replacement met requirements</cite> <cite id="00291047-0">sintering converts organics and locks in metals</cite>. 
- Soil amendment: 
  - Apply only to contaminated or degraded lands needing organic matter; enforce washing/thermal/bio‑remediation to meet metal and PAH leaching limits; integrate with composting/mushroom‑compost biostabilization for hydrocarbon degradation. <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">Purification is required when Hg, Ni, Pb exceed limits</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-2">composting with PAH‑degrading mycelium produces soil conditioners and organic fertilizers</cite>. 

Evidence gaps and how to resolve them
- Direct head‑to‑head cost/GHG footprints across cement, ceramics, and soil pathways are not consistently quantified in accessible studies; however, construction reuse aligns with accepted compliance frameworks and demonstrated performance, whereas soil reuse is constrained by contaminant risk unless treated. Future work should conduct cradle‑to‑gate GHG and techno‑economic analyses benchmarking: (a) cement/concrete (SCM vs. baseline), (b) ceramic tiles/bricks with cuttings vs. virgin bodies, and (c) agronomic yield responses and metal/PAH leaching under field conditions, with sensitivity to pretreatment energy/cost. <cite id="3ef688bc-2">Demonstrated leachability compliance and strength</cite> <cite id="00291047-1">technological viability in ceramics</cite> <cite id="8dfe77d0-0">and regulatory constraints for soil</cite> provide anchors for such comparative assessments. 

Bottom line for your three options:
